# Design Note: Foundry IQ Knowledge Base for Asset Documents

| | |
|---|---|
| **Customer** | AquaNova |
| **Project** | Asset Management Agent |
| **Date** | 2026-04-24 |
| **Author** | Pieter De Smet, Lead AI Architect, Kestrel Consulting |
| **Document type** | Technical design note |
| **Reviewed by** | Kevin Hermans, Jonas Peeters |

## 1. Purpose

Describe how the knowledge base in Foundry IQ is set up for the agent, what it contains, and what we learned from the first evaluation run on 2026-04-17.

## 2. Sources

| Knowledge source | Library | Documents | In phase 1 dev | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Maintenance procedures | Procedures | about 380 | yes | owner: asset management |
| Technical sheets | Technical documentation | about 2,700 | yes | many supplier PDFs, several languages |
| Inspection reports | Inspections (3 libraries) | about 9,200 | from June | needs private networking (ADR-01) |

Each library becomes a separate knowledge source in the knowledge base, so we can tune and refresh them separately and show the planner where an answer came from.

## 3. How the agent uses it

- The agent in Foundry Agent Service calls the knowledge base for any question about procedures, specifications or inspection findings.
- Foundry IQ plans the retrieval: it can split a question into sub-queries ("inspection interval" and "hydrant type in residential street") and combine the results.
- The agent answers only from retrieved content and always lists the sources with a link.
- If nothing relevant is found, the agent says so. The instructions are explicit: no general knowledge about water networks in place of AquaNova's own procedures.

## 4. Metadata

For every document we keep: library, title, document date, asset type (when it can be derived from the folder or file name), and version status. Asset type filtering matters: "inspection interval" has a different answer for hydrants, valves and reservoirs.

# Design Note: Read-Only Agent Tools on Asset Register and Maintenance History

| | |
|---|---|
| **Customer** | AquaNova |
| **Project** | Asset Management Agent |
| **Date** | 2026-05-29 |
| **Author** | Ruben Wouters, Developer, Kestrel Consulting |
| **Document type** | Technical design note |
| **Reviewed by** | Pieter De Smet, Kevin Hermans |

## 1. Purpose

Define the tools that the agent in Foundry Agent Service can call to answer asset-specific questions. In the evaluation set, 22 of 60 questions need these tools (maintenance history, asset lookup, combined questions).

All tools are **read only**. They never write to the asset register or the maintenance history.

## 2. Tool list

| Tool | Question it answers | Priority |
|---|---|---|
| `get_asset_details` | "What is asset X, where is it, what type, what status?" | 1 |
| `get_maintenance_history` | "What was done on asset X, when and why?" | 1 |
| `find_assets_near_location` | "Which valves are within 200 m of this address?" | 2 |
| `get_open_inspection_findings` | "Which open findings exist for asset X or in zone Y?" | 3 |

Priorities agreed with the pilot coordinator on 2026-05-21.

## 3. Contracts

### get_asset_details

- **Input:** `asset_id` (string), optional `asset_type`.
- **Output:** ID, source system (A or B), type (mapped to the common type list), status, installation year, material and diameter (for network assets), coordinates, zone.
- **Behaviour:** if the ID is not found, return "not found" with the input echoed. Never guess a similar ID.

### get_maintenance_history

- **Input:** `asset_id`, optional `from_date`, `to_date`, `max_items` (default 10).
- **Output:** list of interventions: date, type, cause (if structured), free text (shortened to 300 characters), work order number.
- **Behaviour:** newest first. Free text is passed as is; the agent is instructed not to infer causes that are not written.

# Pilot Onboarding: Training Outline for Asset Planners

| | |
|---|---|
| **Customer** | AquaNova |
| **Project** | Asset Management Agent |
| **Date** | 2026-06-12 |
| **Author** | Pieter De Smet, Lead AI Architect, Kestrel Consulting |
| **Document type** | Training material outline |
| **Sessions** | 2026-06-15 and 2026-06-16, 09:30 to 11:00, Leuven (also online) |
| **Audience** | 14 asset planners in the pilot group, pilot coordinator |

## 1. Goal

Planners can use the agent for their daily questions, know what it can and cannot do in this first pilot phase, and know how to give feedback. One session of 90 minutes per group of seven.

## 2. What the pilot offers on day one

- Questions about **maintenance procedures**, **technical sheets** and, from this week, **inspection reports** (except about 1,400 older scanned reports).
- Answers with sources and document dates.
- Not yet: questions about a specific asset's history or location. The tools on the asset register are in development and will be added during the pilot. Until then, the agent says it cannot look up asset records.

We start with documents only on purpose. Planners told us in March that one wrong asset answer would cost more trust than a missing feature.

## 3. Programme

| Time | Block |
|---|---|
| 09:30 | Why this pilot, by Filip Wuyts (first session) or the pilot coordinator (second session) |
| 09:40 | Demo: three real questions from the evaluation set |
| 09:55 | How the agent finds answers: knowledge base, sources, "I don't know" |
| 10:10 | Hands-on: each planner asks five of their own questions |
| 10:35 | Feedback: thumbs up/down, comment, and when to tell the coordinator |
| 10:50 | What's next: tools, timeline, the next evaluation |

## 4. Key messages

1. **Always check the source** for anything you will act on. The agent shows the document and its date. Click it.
2. **"I don't know" is a good answer.** If the agent says it found nothing, it has not guessed.

check the source** for anything you will act on. The agent shows the document and its date. Click it.
2. **"I don't know" is a good answer.** If the agent says it found nothing, it has not guessed.
3. **You only see what you are allowed to see.** The agent respects the same document permissions as the libraries.
4. **Your feedback trains the evaluation, not the model.** Thumbs down and a comment go into the evaluation set; nobody retrains a model on your chats.
5. Do not paste personal data of customers or colleagues into questions.

## 5. Privacy and logging

- Conversations are logged in AquaNova's tenant for 90 days, for quality review by the project team and the pilot coordinator.
- Logs are not used to assess individual planners. This was agreed with Kevin Hermans and AquaNova's privacy officer.

## 6. Hands-on exercise

Each planner gets a sheet with:

- two questions from the evaluation set with known answers,
- three empty lines for their own questions,
- a column to note "useful / not useful / wrong".

The sheets are collected and added to the evaluation set where useful.

## 7. Practical

- Access through the group "AMA pilot"; Kevin has checked all 14 accounts.
- Web chat link on the asset management intranet page.
- Support: the pilot coordinator first, then Pieter (Wednesdays on site).
- Summer: most planners take leave in July or August. We expect lower use then, and plan the first real review in September.

## 8. Materials

- Slides (12) with the demo questions
- One-page "how to ask good questions" (be specific, name the asset type, ask follow-ups)
- FAQ, maintained by the pilot coordinator

# Design Note: Policy-as-code with Azure Policy

| | |
|---|---|
| **Customer** | Fortalis Verzekeringen |
| **Project** | Fortalis Landing Zone |

| **Reviewers** | Kevin Hermans, Enterprise Architect; Fortalis security team |
| **Version** | 0.9 (for design review of 2023-12-05) |

## 1. Goal

Guardrails on the Fortalis platform must be enforced automatically, versioned and reviewable. No portal clicks, no "we agreed in a meeting". This note describes how policies are written, tested, assigned and changed.

## 2. Principles

1. **Every policy is code.** Definitions, initiatives, assignments and exemptions are Bicep files in the platform repository.
2. **Assign at the highest sensible level.** Most assignments sit on the Fortalis root or on the platform, corporate and sandbox management groups. Assignments at subscription level are exceptions and need a reason in the pull request.
3. **Audit first, then deny.** A new policy starts in audit mode for at least two weeks. We look at the compliance results with the owners of non-compliant resources before switching to deny.
4. **Exemptions expire.** Every exemption has an expiry date, an owner and a link to the reason. No permanent exemptions.
5. **Four eyes.** Changes need approval from one person of Kevin's architecture team and, for security-related policies, one person of the security team.

## 3. Policy set

The target set at handover is about 45 assignments, grouped in four initiatives.

| Initiative | Examples | Effect |
|---|---|---|
| Location and residency | allowed regions (two EU regions only), allowed regions for resource groups | deny |
| Tagging | mandatory tags cost centre, owner, data classification, business line; inherit tags from resource group | deny on new spokes, audit elsewhere |

## 1. What happened

On 2024-01-10, the day after the hub was connected to the Brussels datacentre, the deployment of the monitoring components for the shared services spoke failed in the acceptance environment. The pipeline log showed a deny from the **allowed regions** assignment in Azure Policy.

The cause: one of the monitoring services we deploy does not live in a region. It can only be created with the location "global". Our allowed-regions definition lists the two EU regions only, so "global" is denied. In development this went unnoticed, because the allowed-regions policy was still in audit mode there when the monitoring module was first deployed.

## 2. Options

| Option | Pro | Con |
|---|---|---|
| A. Add "global" to the allowed list | Simple | Opens the door for every global resource type, including ones that could process data outside the EU. Security rejected this immediately. |
| B. Exclude the monitoring resource group from the assignment | Simple | Excludes everything in that group, also regional resources. Too broad. |
| C. Scoped exemption for the specific resource type in the monitoring resource group | Narrow, visible, expires | One more file to maintain |
| D. Rewrite the definition to allow "global" only for a list of approved resource types | Precise and reusable | More complex definition, needs testing and review time |

# ADR-01: Hub-spoke network topology

| | |
|---|---|
| **Customer** | Fortalis Verzekeringen |
| **Project** | Fortalis Landing Zone |
| **Document type** | Architecture decision record |
| **Date** | 2023-10-13 |
| **Author** | Jonas Peeters, Cloud Platform Engineer, Kestrel Consulting |
| **Status** | Accepted (design review of 2023-10-10, confirmed by Kevin Hermans) |

## Context

Fortalis Verzekeringen needs a network foundation for all new cloud workloads. Today a few workloads have their own isolated networks, each with its own internet exit and, in one case, its own VPN connection to the Brussels datacentre. There is no central point to inspect traffic, and the security team cannot say with confidence which workloads can reach on-premises systems.

Requirements gathered at the kickoff and in the first design review:

- All outbound internet traffic inspected centrally.
- One controlled connection to the Brussels datacentre.
- Workloads isolated from each other by default.
- New workloads must be able to get a network in days, not weeks.
- The model must be expressible in Bicep and guarded by Azure Policy.

## Options considered

1. **Flat network per workload (status quo).** Fast for each team, but no central inspection and duplicated connectivity. Rejected.
2. **Hub-spoke with a self-managed hub.** A central hub network holds the firewall, the gateway to the datacentre and the private DNS zones. Each workload gets a spoke, peered to the hub, with routes forcing traffic through the hub firewall.
3. **Managed virtual WAN style hub.** Attractive for many regions and branches, but Fortalis has one datacentre and two regions at most. More cost and less control over routing for little benefit.

## Decision

We choose **option 2, hub-spoke with a self-managed hub**.

- One hub per region; for now only the primary EU region gets a hub. The secondary region is reserved in the IP plan.
- Spokes are created from a single Bicep spoke module.

# Design Review Notes: Naming conventions (third round)

| | |
|---|---|
| **Customer** | Fortalis Verzekeringen |
| **Project** | Fortalis Landing Zone |
| **Document type** | Design review notes |
| **Date** | 2023-10-27 |
| **Author** | Jonas Peeters, Cloud Platform Engineer, Kestrel Consulting |
| **Chair** | Kevin Hermans, Enterprise Architect, Fortalis Verzekeringen |

## Attendees

Kevin Hermans (chair), Jonas Peeters, a delegate of the Fortalis cloud team and a delegate of the security team. This review was moved from Tuesday to Friday because of the autumn school holiday week coming up.

## 1. Background

This was the third review on naming. The first two rounds (2023-10-10 and 2023-10-17) agreed on the general pattern but stalled on three points: how to encode the business line, whether to include the region for global resources, and how to name things that have strict length limits. Kevin's position from the start: "We rename nothing after go-live. So we argue now." In hindsight a reasonable position.

## 2. Decisions

**Pattern.** `<type>-<workload>-<env>-<region>-<nn>`, lowercase, hyphen separated. Example: a spoke network for the shared services workload in production in the primary region becomes `vnet-shared-prd-we-01`.

**Business line.** Not part of the name. It goes into a mandatory tag instead, together with cost centre, owner and data classification. Reason: business lines get reorganised, names should not.

**Environments.** Four codes only: `dev`, `tst`, `acc`, `prd`. The cloud team asked for `sbx` for sandboxes; accepted, since sandboxes live in their own management group and are treated differently anyway.

**Region codes.** Two-letter codes for the two allowed EU regions. Global resources use `gl`.

**Short names.** For resources with tight length limits and no hyphens allowed (storage accounts, for example), the pattern is compressed: type abbreviation, workload, environment, two random characters.

# Design Note: Leak Detection and Localisation Model, Version 1

| | |
|---|---|
| **Customer** | AquaNova |
| **Project** | Leak Detection Analytics |
| **Date** | 2025-03-14 |
| **Author** | Amira El Idrissi, ML Engineer, Kestrel Consulting |
| **Document type** | Technical design note |
| **Reviewed with** | Evelien Claes and a GIS analyst, 2025-03-12 |

## 1. Problem

Two questions per morning, for each of the four district metered areas (DMAs) of Noord-Oost:

1. **Detection:** is there a new leak in this DMA?
2. **Localisation:** if so, on which pipe segments is it most likely?

The output is a short list of candidates on the ArcGIS map, each with a confidence score.

## 2. Data

- Daily SCADA export since 2025-01-13, plus 18 months of backfill: inlet flow per DMA, 11 pressure points, pump and reservoir signals.
- Silver and gold features from Bram's Databricks jobs: minimum night flow (02:00–04:00), night-to-day ratio, pressure statistics per point, flow balance per DMA.
- ArcGIS network model of Noord-Oost, after the 37 segment corrections by the GIS team.
- 196 geocoded repair work orders from the last three years, used as labels.

## 3. Detection

Approach: compare each night's minimum night flow with what is expected for that DMA, given season, day of week and temperature.

- An expected-flow model per DMA is trained on nights without known leaks.
- The residual (observed minus expected) is tracked over time. A **sustained step up** over at least three nights is a leak signal. A single high night (flushing, a large consumer, a fire hydrant used) is not.
- Planned works and flushing from asset management's planning are used to mask nights.

On historical data, this flags 71% of repaired leaks at least three days before the repair date, with about one false signal per DMA per month.

## 4. Localisation

When a DMA shows a leak signal, the location is estimated from pressure.

- A leak lowers pressure most at the points closest to it.

about one false signal per DMA per month.

## 4. Localisation

When a DMA shows a leak signal, the location is estimated from pressure.

- A leak lowers pressure most at the points closest to it. For each pressure point, the change in night pressure is compared with the change expected from the extra flow.
- The network model gives, for each pipe segment, how strongly each pressure point "sees" a leak there (a sensitivity table, computed once from the network model in a Python notebook).
- Segments are ranked by how well their sensitivity pattern matches the observed pressure changes.
- Prior per segment from material, age and repair history: cast iron and old PVC get a higher prior.

The top candidate segments that together explain most of the signal form one candidate, shown as a group of segments on the map.

## 5. Training and tracking

- All experiments, models and metrics are tracked in Azure Machine Learning.
- A scheduled pipeline in Azure Machine Learning scores the previous day every morning at 07:00, after the features are ready.
- A retraining pipeline refits the expected-flow models monthly. The GIS team will run this after handover.

## 6. Output to ArcGIS

| Field | Meaning |
|---|---|
| candidate_id | unique per candidate |
| dma | DMA code |
| segments | pipe segments in the candidate area |
| estimated_flow | extra night flow in m³/h |
| confidence | 0 to 1 |
| first_seen | first night of the signal |
| status | new / sent to crew / confirmed / not found |

Crews update the status after validation; the model reads it back for retraining.

## 7. Known limits

- With only 11 pressure points in four DMAs, localisation is coarse in the outer streets. Expect hundreds of metres, not tens.
- Small leaks below about 0.5 m³/h are hard to separate from consumption noise.
- Customer consumption is yearly for most addresses and is not used in the daily model.

## 8. Review with Evelien (2025-03-12)

Evelien and the GIS analyst agreed with the approach.

## 1. Purpose

Agree how field crews will validate leak candidates during the pilot from 2025-04-07 to mid-May, and how their findings come back into the model. Action item from the steering meeting of 2025-02-07.

## 2. How crews search today

The crew leaders explained their routine. A district is flagged by a rising night flow in the weekly check. They drive the district at night or early morning with listening sticks and a ground microphone, starting with streets where they "know" the pipes are bad. On average a crew needs one to three days to find a leak in a district. Customer calls about water on the street or low pressure often come first.

They were sceptical but curious. One crew leader: "If your map sends me to the right three streets, I'll buy you coffee for a month."

## 3. Agreed protocol

1. **Morning list.** Every crew day, the candidate layer in ArcGIS is refreshed by 07:30. The coordinator picks candidates for the day.
2. **Search area.** Crews search the segments of the candidate first, then the connected segments up to the next valve.
3. **Time box.** Maximum half a day per candidate. If nothing is found, status "not found".
4. **Recording.** Crew leaders update the candidate status in ArcGIS on the tablet: *confirmed* (with location of the leak and type: main, service pipe, fitting, hydrant), or *not found*. Free text is optional.
5. **Repair.** Confirmed leaks follow the normal repair work order process. The work order number is added to the candidate.

## Context

The proposal described "flow and pressure data from the SCADA system" without fixing the latency. During discovery we assumed near real time would be possible later, for example to detect burst mains within the hour.

OT security approved only one data path: a nightly export of the agreed tags from the historian through a data diode to a file drop in the OT DMZ, set up by Koen Martens. Since 2025-01-13 this export arrives every morning, together with 18 months of backfilled history.

A near real time flow would need a different design and a new approval round with OT security. Given the seven weeks the first approval took, that is not feasible within this project.

## Options

1. **Accept daily data for the whole project.** Design all models and the ArcGIS layer around a morning refresh.
2. **Ask for a second, near real time flow now.** New approval round, unknown duration, risk to the pilot in April.
3. **Daily data now, design so a faster feed can be plugged in later.** Same as option 1, with the ingestion and features written so that the time window is a parameter.

## Decision

Option 3.

- The lakehouse in Microsoft Fabric loads the nightly file at 06:00.
- Databricks jobs compute night-flow and pressure features for the previous day by 06:45.
- The model in Azure Machine Learning scores leak candidates by 07:15.
- The ArcGIS candidate layer is refreshed before 07:30, so crews see it at the start of their day.
- Feature jobs take the window length as a parameter, so a shorter window can be used if a faster feed is ever approved.

## Consequences

## Consequences

**Positive**

- Night flow, the strongest leak signal for small and medium leaks, is measured once per night anyway. Daily data loses almost nothing for this.
- Simple, robust, no dependency on a permanent connection.
- No inbound path to the OT network, in line with AquaNova's OT policy.

**Negative**

- Large bursts are not detected faster than today's SCADA alarms. That stays with the control room, as it is now. Leak detection analytics is about the leaks nobody sees.
- A failed nightly export means one day without candidates. Bram adds monitoring on the file drop.
- Pressure transients can only be analysed the next day.

- Procedure for adding tags to the export without a full new approval round (Koen).

# Lunch and Learn: Building a Teams Bot That People Actually Use

| | |
|---|---|
| **Organisation** | Kestrel Consulting (internal) |
| **Date** | 2025-04-25, 12:15 to 13:15 |

## Introduction

First kennisdeling session of 2025, and my first talk at Kestrel. Elien convinced me that a junior perspective is useful, so here it is: what I learned in three months of building the Teams bot front end for the **Scaldis Ops Copilot**. The copilot answers questions from terminal staff about SOPs and work instructions stored in SharePoint, using Azure AI Search for retrieval and Azure OpenAI to write the answer. My part is the bot in Microsoft Teams, the piece that users actually see.

## 1. Teams is the user interface, so respect Teams

Shift leaders at a terminal do not want a new app. They already live in Teams on a laptop in the office or on their phone on the quay. That is the whole reason for choosing a bot. But it also means users expect the bot to behave like a colleague in a chat:
- answer in the language of the question (Dutch, French or English at Scaldis)
- short first answer, details on request
- no walls of text on a phone screen

Elien and I paired on the answer layout. We ended up with a three-part card: the answer in at most five sentences, the source procedure with a link, and two buttons ("helpful" and "not helpful").

## 2. Always show the source

The single most appreciated feature in the pilot is the link to the SOP. Planners told us they do not mind if the bot is sometimes vague, as long as they can click through to the procedure and check. A bot without sources would not be trusted in an environment where a wrong procedure can mean a safety incident.

## 3. Things that cost me time

as they can click through to the procedure and check. A bot without sources would not be trusted in an environment where a wrong procedure can mean a safety incident.

## 3. Things that cost me time

- **App policies.** The bot did not show up for some users because of the customer's Teams app setup policies. That is not a code problem; it needs the customer's Teams administrator. Ask for the app policy rules on day one.
- **Authentication.** Single sign-on in a Teams bot has more moving parts than I expected. Write down the consent and redirect settings per environment; you will forget them.
- **Timeouts.** Retrieval plus generation sometimes takes several seconds. Teams expects a fast response, so the bot first sends a typing indicator and then updates the message. Without it, users ask the same question twice.
- **Card features on mobile.** The mobile Teams client supports a slightly different set of features than desktop. Test on a phone early.

## 4. Logging and feedback

Every question and the feedback button click are logged, without the user's name, with the sources used and the response time. Pieter reviews the "not helpful" answers with Nathalie Dumont's team every two weeks. Most of the bad answers so far trace back to outdated or duplicate SOP versions, not to the model. It turns out that content quality is half of the job.

## 5. What I would tell another junior

1. Ask the customer's Teams administrator for a test tenant or a test policy in week one.
2. Build the feedback buttons in the first sprint, not the last.
3. Pair with UX. My first card design was technically correct and nobody liked it.
4. Read the existing documents. Half the questions users ask are already answered in an SOP; the other half show which SOPs are missing.

## Questions from the room

- *Can the bot be reused for other customers?* The front-end part, largely yes. We are keeping the card templates and the logging generic.

| | |
|---|---|
| **Organisation** | Kestrel Consulting (internal) |

## Purpose

Second "kennisdeling" session of 2025. This time we chose three projects where something went sideways, to see what we can change in the way we start and run projects. About 18 colleagues attended, 4 remotely. The rule was the usual one: no blame, focus on what we would do differently.

## 1. Scaldis Ops Copilot: the late security review

*Presented by Pieter De Smet*

- The copilot answers questions on SOPs in SharePoint through a Teams bot. The customer's IT Security Officer, Wim Goossens, did his formal review only after the pilot was running.
- His main finding: answers must respect document-level permissions in SharePoint. Restricted procedures had come into scope halfway, and our index did not trim on permissions.
- Result: rework of the index and query layer, and the go-live moved from 1 July to 15 September.
- Discussion: several people said that on RAG projects "security review before go-live" is too late by definition, because permissions shape the architecture. Wim was right; we just involved him too late.

**Takeaways**
- Put the security officer's architecture review in sprint 1 of every project that indexes company documents.
- Ask early which content is restricted, even if it is "not in scope yet".

## 2. Fortalis Claims Triage: scope creep on a fixed price

*Presented by Thomas Maes*

- Fixed price project for automated triage of incoming claims. Midway, the customer asked to add water damage claim types. It was handled with change request CR-07, approved by their sponsor, but only after a lot of work had already started informally.

for regression testing, but for text that people sign or act on, domain experts must judge it. The **Discharge Letter Summarisation** project at Mediva, which closed in October, is our reference:

- The evaluation ran over eight weeks with **12 physicians** from two departments.
- Each physician first wrote letters as usual during a **baseline period**, then with the generated draft.
- Drafts were rated on a simple scale ("usable with minor edits", "usable with major edits", "not usable") and the time per letter was measured, not asked.
- Headline result: about **9 minutes saved per discharge letter**.

What made it convincing for the sponsor was the baseline. Surveys asking "how much time does this save you?" give optimistic and inconsistent answers. Measure before and after.

## 4. Automate the regression run

- Every change to prompts, retrieval, model version or training data triggers a run of the full evaluation set.
- Results are stored per run with the configuration that produced them, so we can say which change made it better or worse.
- Use an LLM-as-judge only as a pre-filter, calibrated against human ratings on a sample. Report the agreement rate.

## 5. Look at the errors, not only the score

- Read at least 20 failed items after every significant run. Classify them: data problem, retrieval problem, model problem, unclear reference.
- Unclear references are common. Fix the evaluation set, and note it in the version log.
- Report errors by segment (document type, department, class). An average hides the segment that matters.

## 6. Keep evaluating after go-live

- Monitor input drift: new document layouts, new claim types, seasonal effects. Data changes; models do not adapt by themselves.
- Collect user feedback with a single click on each answer or prediction, and review it on a fixed rhythm.

# Engineering Guideline: Coding Standards

| | |
|---|---|
| **Organisation** | Kestrel Consulting (internal) |
| **Date** | 2025-02-14 |
| **Author** | Pieter De Smet, Lead AI Architect |
| **Document type** | Engineering guideline, version 2.0 |
| **Applies to** | Application, data and ML code written by Kestrel |

## Why

We hand over almost everything we build. The customer's team will read our code long after we have left, often without us in the room. Code that is consistent, tested and boring to read is a feature. This guideline replaces the 2023 version, mainly to add rules for code that calls language models.

## 1. Languages and project setup

- **Python** for data, ML and back-end services. **TypeScript** for front ends, Teams apps and lightweight APIs where the team prefers it.
- Every repository starts from the internal template: folder layout, formatter, linter, type checking, test setup and pipeline definition included. Do not start from an empty folder.
- Dependencies are pinned with a lock file. Upgrades are a deliberate pull request, not a side effect.

## 2. Style

- Formatting is automatic. Nobody discusses whitespace in a review.
- Linter warnings fail the pipeline. If a rule really does not fit, disable it in the configuration with a comment, not inline all over the code.
- Type hints in Python on every public function. Strict mode in TypeScript.
- Names in English, also for customers with Dutch or French domain terms. Keep a glossary in the README for domain words that have no good translation.

## 3. Structure

- Small modules with one responsibility. A file longer than about 400 lines is a signal, not a crime.
- Configuration through environment variables and a typed settings object. No hard-coded endpoints, no keys in code.
- Business rules (deduplication rules, routing thresholds, class definitions) live in one place and are readable by a non-developer. Customers will ask to change them.

## 4. Tests

- Unit tests for business logic.

# Tech Talk: Permission-Aware Retrieval

| | |
|---|---|
| **Organisation** | Kestrel Consulting (internal) |
| **Date** | 2025-11-07, 16:00 to 17:00 |
| **Location** | Kestrel office Ghent and Teams |
| **Author / presenter** | Pieter De Smet, Lead AI Architect |
| **Document type** | Internal tech talk notes |

## Why this talk

A retrieval system that ignores permissions is a data leak with a nice chat interface. I learned that the expensive way on the **Scaldis Ops Copilot**, which went live on **2025-09-22**. This talk explains what went wrong, how we fixed it, and how we design for it from now on. It complements the June lessons-learned session, which covered the project management side.

## The case in short

- The copilot answers questions from terminal staff in Microsoft Teams, based on SOPs and work instructions stored in SharePoint. Retrieval runs on Azure AI Search; answers are generated with Azure OpenAI.
- Halfway through the project, restricted procedures (customs, security, some incident procedures) came into scope.
- The customer's IT Security Officer, Wim Goossens, did his formal review in spring, when the pilot was already running. His finding: the index did not respect **document-level permissions**. A user could get an answer based on a procedure they were not allowed to open in SharePoint.
- Go-live was re-planned to 2025-09-15. After a final re-test following a renamed SharePoint group, we went live a week later, on 2025-09-22, with a clean sign-off.
- In the first month **340 users** used the copilot.

Wim was right. The lesson is not "security reviews slow you down" but "security shapes the architecture, so it belongs in sprint 1".

## How permission trimming works

1. **Index the permissions with the content.** For every document chunk, store the identifiers of the groups and users allowed to read the source document.
2. **Resolve the user at query time.** The bot knows who is asking.

# Policy Note: Identity, Access and Secrets on Customer Work

| | |
|---|---|
| **Organisation** | Kestrel Consulting (internal) |
| **Date** | 2026-04-17 |
| **Author** | Jonas Peeters, Cloud Platform Engineer |
| **Document type** | Internal security policy note, version 1.0 |
| **Approved by** | Lotte Willems |

## Purpose

More of our work now involves AI agents that read documents and call tools on customer systems. That raises the stakes on identity and access: an agent with too many rights is an attacker's dream. This note sets the minimum rules for how Kestrel colleagues handle identities, access and secrets in customer and internal environments. Customer policies that are stricter always take precedence.

## 1. Our own accounts

- MFA on every account, phishing-resistant methods where the customer supports them.
- Use the guest or member account the customer gives you, never a shared account. If a customer proposes a shared "kestrel" account, politely refuse and explain why.
- Privileged roles only through just-in-time activation, time-limited, with a reason. No standing owner rights on production subscriptions, also not "just for the duration of the project".
- When you leave an engagement, ask the customer to remove your access, and confirm it in writing. Put it in the handover checklist.

# Engineering Guideline: Bicep Conventions

| | |
|---|---|
| **Organisation** | Kestrel Consulting (internal) |
| **Date** | 2023-11-10 |
| **Author** | Jonas Peeters, Cloud Platform Engineer |
| **Document type** | Engineering guideline, version 1.0 |
| **Applies to** | All infrastructure-as-code written by Kestrel |

## Why this guideline

Bicep is our standard for infrastructure as code on Azure. Until now every project had its own style, which makes handover to customer IT teams harder and makes it difficult to reuse modules. This guideline sets the minimum conventions. It is short on purpose; where it is silent, use common sense and the existing modules in the internal template repository.

## 1. Repository layout

```
infra/
  main.bicep            # entry point per environment scope
  main.<env>.bicepparam # one parameter file per environment
  modules/              # project-specific modules
  shared/               # copied from the internal template, do not edit in place
```

- One `main.bicep` per deployment scope (subscription or resource group). Do not mix scopes in one file.
- Shared modules are copied with a version tag in the header comment. If you improve one, contribute it back to the template repository.

## 2. Naming

- Resource names follow `<type>-<workload>-<env>-<region>-<nn>`, for example `vnet-hub-prd-weu-01`. Type abbreviations follow the list in the template repository.
- Customers often have their own naming standard. **Theirs wins.** Put the naming logic in one module (`naming.bicep`) so it can be swapped.
- Parameters and variables in camelCase, no abbreviations except the usual ones (`env`, `rg`, `vnet`).

## 3. Parameters

- Every parameter gets a `@description`. Use `@allowed` for environment and SKU parameters.
- No secrets in parameter files, ever. Reference them at deployment time from the customer's secret store.
- Defaults only for values that are truly the same in every environment.

## 4. Identity and access

in parameter files, ever. Reference them at deployment time from the customer's secret store.
- Defaults only for values that are truly the same in every environment.

## 4. Identity and access

- Role assignments are part of the code, not clicked in the portal afterwards. Use Microsoft Entra ID groups as principals, not individual users.
- Prefer managed identities for service-to-service access. A connection string with a key is an exception that needs a comment explaining why.
- Use `guid()` with stable inputs for role assignment names so redeployments are idempotent.

## 5. Policy as code

Governance rules belong in Azure Policy definitions and assignments, deployed from the same repository as the infrastructure. On the **Fortalis Landing Zone** engagement, which is running now, the hub-spoke landing zone is set up exactly this way: policy definitions, initiatives and assignments are all in Bicep, versioned and reviewed like any other code. Exemptions are also in code, with an expiry date and a reason. That makes the yearly governance review a matter of reading a pull request history instead of a portal hunt.

Default policy set for new environments (adapt per customer):
- allowed regions (EU only, unless agreed otherwise)
- mandatory tags: `owner`, `costCenter`, `environment`, `workload`
- deny public IP addresses on network interfaces in spokes
- diagnostic settings to the central log workspace

## 6. Deployment

- Deploy through a pipeline with a what-if step before every apply. The what-if output is attached to the pull request.
- Production deployments require a second reviewer and are never done from a laptop.
- Use named, tagged deployments so it is clear which deployment created which resource.

## 7. Linting and review

- The Bicep linter runs with our shared configuration; warnings are treated as errors in the pipeline.
- Every module has a short README with inputs, outputs and an example.

# Lunch and Learn: Dashboards on the Wall

| | |
|---|---|
| **Organisation** | Kestrel Consulting (internal) |
| **Date** | 2023-12-08, 12:15 to 13:15 |
| **Location** | Kestrel office Ghent, big room (sandwiches provided) |
| **Author / presenter** | Elien Jacobs, UX and Frontend Developer |
| **Document type** | Internal session notes |

## Summary of the talk

This lunch session was about one lesson from the **Bed Capacity Dashboard** at Mediva Care Group, which closed on 2023-11-30: a dashboard that nobody opens is not a dashboard, it is a report nobody reads.

### The situation

The dashboard was adopted quickly by the day shifts and the bed management office. But the **night shift nurses kept using the whiteboard** at the nursing station. Their reasoning was not resistance to change. At three in the morning, with two nurses for a whole ward, nobody walks to a PC, logs in, and opens a report to see which beds are free. The whiteboard is on the wall, in the corridor, always on.

### What we did

Instead of more training, I designed a **large-screen view per ward**:
- one page, no filters, no navigation
- beds as coloured tiles (free, occupied, expected discharge, blocked), with large room numbers
- auto-refresh, no login needed on the screen itself (the device is managed by hospital IT)
- readable from about five metres, also with tired eyes

We tested it for two weeks on one internal medicine ward. After that the hospital's IT team ordered wall screens for the other wards. Some wards kept a small whiteboard for notes that do not belong in any system, and that is fine.

### Design lessons

1. **Observe the moment of use.** We interviewed head nurses during the day. We should have spent one night on a ward during discovery. Lotte has added this to the discovery checklist for operational dashboards.
2. **Distance changes everything.** On a wall screen, font size, contrast and the number of elements are the design.

# Tech Talk: Trusting Operational Event Data

| | |
|---|---|
| **Organisation** | Kestrel Consulting (internal) |
| **Date** | 2024-04-12, 15:00 to 16:00 (kennisdeling session, moved from March) |
| **Location** | Kestrel office Ghent and Teams |
| **Author / presenter** | Sofie Claes, Senior Data Engineer |
| **Document type** | Internal tech talk notes |

## Context

This talk used the **Container Dwell-Time Forecasting** project at Scaldis Logistics, which closed on 2024-03-29, as a case. The project forecasts how long import containers stay on the terminal yard. The forecast is only as good as the event history behind it, and the event history came from the terminal operating system (TOS).

## The problem: events that lie

The model needs, for every container, a clean sequence of gate-in, yard moves and gate-out. In the raw data we found:

- **Duplicate gate-in events**: the same container registered twice within minutes, sometimes with a slightly different timestamp, sometimes on a different lane.
- **Missing gate-in events**: containers that appear in yard moves without ever having entered the terminal.
- Late corrections: an event corrected days later by a clerk, overwriting the original.

A dwell time computed on such data is simply wrong, and a model trained on it learns the wrong lesson.

## What we did

1. **Deduplication rules.** Two gate-in events for the same container within a configurable time window are one event; the first one counts, unless the second is a correction. The rules are written down in plain language with the operations team, then implemented in the pipeline.
2. **Inferred events.** For a missing gate-in, we infer the time from the first yard move and flag the record. The model sees the flag as a feature, and the monitoring counts them.
3. **A data contract (v1.0)** for TOS events: field definitions, allowed values, the deduplication rules and what happens when the schema changes.

# Policy Note: Handling Customer Data under GDPR

| | |
|---|---|
| **Organisation** | Kestrel Consulting (internal) |
| **Date** | 2024-04-26 |
| **Author** | Lotte Willems, Managing Partner |
| **Document type** | Internal policy note, version 2.0 (replaces version 1.3 of 2022) |
| **Applies to** | All Kestrel staff and subcontractors working under Kestrel contracts |

## 1. Why an update

Our work has shifted from dashboards and pipelines towards AI on documents and text. That means we see more personal data, and sometimes special categories such as health data. This note sets out what every colleague must do. It does not replace the data processing agreement with each customer; where the agreement is stricter, the agreement wins.

## 2. Our role

In almost all engagements the customer is the **controller** and Kestrel is a **processor**. We process personal data only on documented instructions of the customer, for the purpose of the engagement, and only for as long as needed.

## 3. Before any personal data is touched

1. A signed data processing agreement is in place.
2. The customer has confirmed whether a **DPIA** (data protection impact assessment) is needed. For any processing of health data, or large-scale processing with AI models, assume it is needed until the customer's DPO says otherwise.
3. Data minimisation is agreed: which fields, which period, which population.
4. The location of processing is agreed. Default: EU regions only.

A practical example. On the **Discharge Letter Summarisation** engagement at Mediva Care Group, the DPIA had to be completed before any patient data could be processed. The start moved six weeks, from the planned 2024-02-05 to **2024-03-18**. The outcome, agreed with Mediva's DPO, was clear: pseudonymisation of the content before every call to the Azure OpenAI model, and no patient data leaving the EU. In hindsight, the DPIA should have started before the contract was signed.

# FinOps Tips: Cost Hygiene on Customer and Internal Subscriptions

| | |
|---|---|
| **Organisation** | Kestrel Consulting (internal) |
| **Date** | 2024-09-27 |
| **Author** | Jonas Peeters, Cloud Platform Engineer |
| **Document type** | Internal guideline (FinOps tips, part 1) |

## Why this note

Twice this year a customer asked us, a bit pointedly, why their development environment cost more than production. Both times the answer was idle compute left running by the project team. Nobody was careless on purpose; it is just easy to forget. Below are the habits I want every project to follow. None of them take more than a few minutes.

## 1. Tag everything from day one

Every resource carries at least `owner`, `costCenter`, `environment` and `workload`. Our Bicep templates set these by default and the policy set denies untagged resources in new environments. Tags are what make a cost report readable for the customer's finance team. Without them, every cost review starts with "what is this?".

## 2. Budgets and alerts per environment

- Create a budget per resource group or subscription for each environment, at the start of the project.
- Alerts at 50%, 80% and 100% of the monthly budget, sent to the engagement lead and to a customer contact.
- The first alert is not a crisis. It is a reason to look.

## 3. Switch it off

The biggest savings are always the same:
- **Compute instances and notebooks**: configure idle shutdown (30 to 60 minutes) on every personal compute instance.
- **Spark clusters**: auto-termination after 20 to 30 minutes of inactivity, and a cluster policy that limits node types and the maximum number of workers in development. Nobody needs a 16-node cluster to test a notebook.
- **Capacity-based services**: if the service can be paused, schedule a pause outside working hours and at weekends in development and test.
- **Virtual machines** for jump hosts or tooling: auto-shutdown at 19:00.

# Workshop Notes: Claims intake and triage process mapping

| | |
|---|---|
| **Customer** | Fortalis Verzekeringen |
| **Project** | Claims Triage Automation |
| **Document type** | Workshop notes |

| **Author** | Thomas Maes, Project Manager, Kestrel Consulting |
| **Participants** | Laura Vermeulen; two senior claims handlers; one intake team lead; Amira El Idrissi; Thomas Maes |

## 1. Goal

Map how a claim moves from arrival to the first handler today, agree the definitions the model will learn (type, complexity, urgency) and identify where automation adds most value. Full day at the Fortalis office, with a long sheet of brown paper and too many sticky notes.

## 2. Current process (as-is)

1. **Arrival.** Claims arrive through three channels: the central intake mailbox (about half), the broker upload function (about a third), and the customer portal (the rest). Brokers often send the same claim by mail and upload, which creates duplicates.
2. **Registration.** An intake employee creates or finds the claim in the claims management system, links the policy and attaches the documents. Average 6 to 8 minutes per claim, much longer when the policy number is missing.
3. **Sorting.** The same employee opens the documents, decides the claim type and assigns a queue. For doubtful cases they ask a senior handler.
4. **Urgency.** Set by gut feeling. There is a flag "urgent" in the system, but each team uses it differently.
5. **First handler.** Picks the claim from the queue, often re-reads everything, and in about one in eight cases sends it back because it is in the wrong queue.

Observations from the handlers: the sorting step itself is quick for an experienced person; what costs time is opening and reading poorly scanned documents, and chasing missing policy numbers.

## 3. Definitions agreed

**Claim type (first release):** motor (own damage), motor (third party), fire, theft from home, theft of vehicle, other.

documents, and chasing missing policy numbers.

## 3. Definitions agreed

**Claim type (first release):** motor (own damage), motor (third party), fire, theft from home, theft of vehicle, other. "Other" is a legitimate answer and goes to the human triage queue.

**Complexity:** simple, standard, complex. Complex means: injury mentioned, more than one party, estimated amount above the threshold Laura's team uses today for expert involvement, or signs of litigation.

**Urgency:** three levels.
- **U1** - the customer cannot use their home or vehicle, or there is a risk of further damage (open roof, broken door lock).
- **U2** - normal handling within the service level.
- **U3** - no time pressure (for example, a minor scratch reported for information).

This replaces the "every fire claim is urgent" rule. Laura will confirm the definitions in writing; they will be captured as a scope clarification in the change log, without cost impact.

## 4. Where automation helps most

| Step | Automation potential | Comment |
|---|---|---|
| Duplicate detection across channels | High | Same policy, same date of loss, within 48 hours |
| Field extraction (policy number, date and place of loss, amount) | High | Biggest time saver for intake |
| Claim type | High for motor and theft, medium for fire | Fire claims often mix several damage types |
| Complexity | Medium | Injury mentions are hard to catch in free text |
| Urgency | Medium | Depends on details in the customer's description |

## 5. Pain points not in scope

- Poor scan quality from some brokers. Not solvable by the project; Laura will raise it with the broker account managers.
- Claims reported by phone and typed in by the call centre. These arrive in the system without documents and are excluded from the first release.

# ADR-01: Confidence threshold and the human triage queue

| | |
|---|---|
| **Customer** | Fortalis Verzekeringen |
| **Project** | Claims Triage Automation |
| **Document type** | Architecture decision record |
| **Date** | 2024-05-08 |
| **Author** | Amira El Idrissi, ML Engineer, Kestrel Consulting |
| **Decided with** | Laura Vermeulen (product owner), Thomas Maes, Jonas Peeters |
| **Status** | Accepted |

## Context

The triage model predicts three things for each incoming claim: claim type, complexity and urgency (U1 to U3), each with a probability. Some claims will be clear, others ambiguous. We need a rule for when the system routes a claim on its own and when a person decides. The rule must be understandable for the claims team, adjustable without retraining, and safe for urgent cases.

At the kickoff it was agreed that claims the model cannot classify with enough confidence always go to people. This ADR makes that concrete.

## Options considered

1. **One global threshold on the type prediction.** Simple, but ignores urgency: a confidently classified fire claim with an uncertain urgency could be routed as U2 while the family is sleeping at a neighbour's.
2. **Separate thresholds per output, all must pass.** Safer. Lower auto-routing rate, because three conditions must hold at the same time.
3. **Learned "route or defer" model.** Elegant, but hard to explain and to tune by the business. Rejected for the first release.

## Decision

**Option 2, separate thresholds per output, all must pass**, plus a set of hard rules that always defer.

A claim is auto-routed only if:

- the type probability is at least **0.85**, and
- the complexity probability is at least **0.80**, and
- the urgency probability is at least **0.80**, or the predicted urgency is U1 (see below), and
- none of the hard rules applies.

**Hard rules (always to the human triage queue):**

- Predicted type is "other".
- Policy number could not be extracted or does not match an active policy.

# Labelling Guidelines v1.0: Complexity and urgency

| | |
|---|---|
| **Customer** | Fortalis Verzekeringen |
| **Project** | Claims Triage Automation |
| **Document type** | Guideline / working instruction |
| **Date** | 2024-05-29 |
| **Author** | Amira El Idrissi, ML Engineer, Kestrel Consulting |
| **Approved by** | Laura Vermeulen, Claims Operations Manager |
| **For** | Claims handlers labelling historical claims |

## 1. Why this document

After the first three weeks of labelling, the two labellers agreed on urgency in only about two thirds of the 50 claims they both labelled. Most disagreements were not about the facts but about the rule being applied. In the calibration session of 2024-05-23 we went through every disagreement together. This document captures the outcome so that every labeller, including the colleague joining on Wednesdays, applies the same rules.

## 2. General rules

1. **Label what was known at intake.** Look only at the documents and text available when the claim arrived. Do not use information from later correspondence or the final settlement, even if you remember the case.
2. **When in doubt, choose "unsure".** An "unsure" label is useful. A guessed label harms the model.
3. **One claim, one label set.** If a file contains two claims (for example a car theft with damage to the garage), label the main claim and add a note.
4. **Do not correct the claim type here.** Claim type comes from the system. If you think it is wrong, tick "type doubtful".

## 3. Complexity

| Label | Use when | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| Simple | One party, clear cause, no injury, estimated amount below the expert threshold | Broken car window, stolen bicycle from a shed |
| Standard | Normal investigation needed, possibly a second party, amount below the expert threshold | Parking damage with a known third party |
| Complex | Any of: injury mentioned, more than two parties, amount above the expert threshold, signs of litigation, a lawyer in copy |

# ADR-01: Networking and Identity for the Foundry Project

| | |
|---|---|
| **Customer** | AquaNova |
| **Project** | Asset Management Agent |
| **Date** | 2026-02-27 |
| **Author** | Jonas Peeters, Cloud Platform Engineer, Kestrel Consulting |
| **Document type** | Architecture decision record |
| **Status** | Accepted by Kevin Hermans, IT Architect, on 2026-02-26 |

## Context

The agent runs in a Microsoft Foundry project in AquaNova's Azure tenant, built on Foundry Agent Service, with a Foundry IQ knowledge base over AquaNova's document libraries and tools that read the asset register and maintenance history.

Kevin's requirements from the kickoff:

1. No public endpoints for the Foundry resources in the target state.
2. Planners only see documents they are allowed to see.
3. Read-only access to source systems, with minimal rights.
4. All configuration as code, so the setup can be rebuilt and reviewed.

AquaNova already runs a hub network in Azure with a connection to the office network. The asset register view is reachable only from inside AquaNova's network.

## Options considered

**A. Private networking from day one.** No public access at all. Safest, but the hub team has a two- to three-week lead time for new network integrations, which would block development in March.

**B. Public endpoints with IP restrictions permanently.** Simple, but against Kevin's requirement 1.

**C. Phased.** Development on restricted public endpoints (Kestrel and AquaNova office IP ranges only) with a limited set of documents, while private networking is built in parallel. Inspection reports and the asset register only after private networking is in place.

## Decision

Option C.

- **Phase 1 (March to May 2026):** Foundry project with restricted public access. Only a copy of maintenance procedures and technical sheets classified as internal (selection approved by Kevin) and an anonymised sample of the asset extracts. No inspection reports, no connection to the asset register.

procedures and technical sheets classified as internal (selection approved by Kevin) and an anonymised sample of the asset extracts. No inspection reports, no connection to the asset register.
- **Phase 2 (from June 2026):** private connectivity for the Foundry resources, the knowledge base storage and the tool backend through AquaNova's hub network. Public access switched off resource by resource, with Kevin's sign-off for each.

**Identity**

- Planners sign in with their AquaNova accounts. Access to the web chat through one group "AMA pilot".
- The knowledge base respects document-level permissions of the source libraries. A planner without access to a document does not get answers based on it.
- The tool backend reads the asset register and maintenance history with its own service identity, read-only on the views it needs, nothing else.
- Kestrel engineers get time-limited guest access, reviewed monthly by Kevin.

**Configuration as code**

All resources are described in infrastructure-as-code templates in AquaNova's repository. Changes go through a pull request reviewed by Kevin or his deputy.

## Consequences

- Development can start in March without waiting for the hub team.
- Real data arrives later than in the SOW planning; tools that need the asset register can only be tested end to end from June. This is an explicit risk for sprint block 3.
- Switching off public access later needs a small test plan per resource.
- Document-level permissions must be tested with at least two planners with different access before the pilot.

## 1. Scope of this note

How the triage solution is deployed in the project spoke of the Fortalis landing zone and how a claim flows through the components. The model itself is described in the model card by Amira; routing rules are in ADR-01.

## 2. Components

| Component | Service | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| Intake flow | Azure Logic Apps | Picks up claims from the intake mailbox, the broker uploads and the portal export folder |
| Triage flow | Azure Logic Apps | Calls extraction and classification, applies thresholds and hard rules, writes to the claims system |
| Extraction | Azure AI Document Intelligence | Document type classifier plus custom extraction models (claim form, repair quote, police report) |
| Classification | Azure Machine Learning | Managed online endpoint hosting the triage model; training pipelines and model registry |
| Storage | Storage account in the spoke | Incoming documents, extraction results, audit trail |
| Secrets | Spoke secrets store | Connection secrets that cannot yet be replaced by workload identities |

All services have private endpoints in the spoke and resolve through the hub DNS zones. There are no public endpoints. The infrastructure is deployed with the landing zone's infrastructure-as-code modules and pipeline, so the Fortalis guardrails (allowed regions, mandatory tags, diagnostic settings) apply without exceptions.

## 3. Flow of one claim

1. **Pick-up.** The intake flow polls the intake mailbox every two minutes and receives broker uploads and portal exports as they arrive. Each claim gets a correlation ID.

## 3. Flow of one claim

1. **Pick-up.** The intake flow polls the intake mailbox every two minutes and receives broker uploads and portal exports as they arrive. Each claim gets a correlation ID.
2. **Duplicate check.** Same policy number and date of loss within 48 hours through another channel: the claim is marked as possible duplicate (hard rule, see ADR-01).
3. **Document classification.** Every attachment goes through the Document Intelligence classifier. Photos are kept but not analysed.
4. **Extraction.** Claim forms, repair quotes and police reports go to their custom model. Fields below the field-level confidence threshold are left empty, never guessed.
5. **Classification.** The triage flow sends extracted fields and the free text description to the online endpoint in Azure Machine Learning and receives type, complexity and urgency with probabilities.
6. **Decision.** Thresholds and hard rules are evaluated in the triage flow. Configuration is stored as a versioned parameter file.
7. **Write-back.** Through the claims system write interface (expected mid-August, see risk log). Until then, results go to a stub that mimics the interface.
8. **Audit.** Every step writes to the audit trail: input documents, extracted fields, model version, probabilities, decision and reason.

## 1. Why monthly retraining

Claims change with the seasons. After the autumn storms of 2024, claims arrived with different wording, documents and volumes, and the override rate doubled in a few weeks. A retraining on recent claims restored quality. To avoid waiting for the next drop, the triage model is retrained every month on the latest labelled claims.

- **First Tuesday of the month:** the operator starts the retraining pipeline in Azure Machine Learning.
- **By Thursday:** evaluation report available to the model owner.

## Format

Two hours at the Fortalis office, one week before closure. First hour Kestrel team only, second hour with Laura. Classic format: what went well, what did not, what we do differently next time. Every point needed a concrete example.

## What went well

- **Building on the landing zone.** The spoke was ready in the first week. No discussion about networks, regions or tags. Jonas: "The guardrails meant we never had to argue about security from scratch."
- **Privacy review before real data.** Holding the DPO review before real claims entered acceptance meant no rework. The pseudonymisation rules written then were reused for the monthly retraining.
- **Labelling guidelines and calibration.** Agreement between labellers on urgency went from about two thirds to 84% after one calibration session and a two-page guideline.
- **Proposal mode pilot.** Running on live intake for two months before auto-routing gave us real override figures and showed the storm drift before it could do harm.
- **Overrides as labels.** Designing the handler screen to store every correction with the original prediction made the December retraining possible in days instead of weeks.
- **Load test.** Found the real bottleneck (extraction, not the claims system) and the urgent-claims-in-a-burst problem early.

## What did not go well

- **Water damage started before it was costed.** We said "we'll have a look" in the sprint 9 review and spent about four days before CR-07 was written. Marc was fair about it, but it put the project in amber for the rest of its life. (Thomas)

## 1. Question

Why did the override rate in the live pilot rise from about 9% (acceptance sessions in October) to about 18% at the end of November and in the first week of December, and what do we do about it before auto-routing goes live?

## 2. What we looked at

- All 2,960 overrides from 2024-11-04 to 2024-12-08, with the original prediction and the handler's correction.

## 3. Findings

**3.1 It is the data, not the software.** Extraction quality on claim forms and repair quotes is unchanged. Technical deferrals are below 1%. The classification endpoint returns the same results for the same input. The problem is the input itself.

**3.2 Storm-related claims dominate the overrides.** About 70% of the overridden claims relate to storm damage after the autumn storms: roof damage, fallen trees on houses and cars, water infiltration through a damaged roof. These claims:

- were three to four times more frequent per week than in the same weeks of the historical extract;
- have shorter descriptions (median 19 words against 46), often typed on a phone;
- carry more photos and fewer documents, and a new document type: the roofer's or contractor's quote;
- use vocabulary the model rarely saw ("dakpannen", "tuiles", "boom omgewaaid", "chute d'arbre").

## 1. Summary

The Bed Capacity Dashboard project ran from 2023-05-08 to 2023-11-30 and closes today as planned. Mediva Care Group now has a single, near real-time view of bed occupancy, expected discharges and admissions in the pipeline, and the dashboard is in daily use on all three campuses. The project was delivered within the fixed price of EUR 60,000.

The sponsor on the Mediva side was Jeroen Lambrecht, IT Manager. I acted as engagement lead and project manager for Kestrel myself, which suited a small, tightly scoped engagement like this one.

## 2. Scope and solution

The goal was to replace the morning phone round, in which bed managers called every ward to collect occupancy figures, with a shared dashboard.

- **Data layer:** Azure Synapse Analytics pulls admission, transfer and discharge events from the hospital information system every 15 minutes and consolidates them into a bed-level model per campus, ward and room. Sofie Claes, Senior Data Engineer, built the pipelines and the occupancy model, including the logic for "blocked" beds (isolation, maintenance) that the source system records inconsistently.
- **Reporting layer:** Power BI reports on top of Synapse, with a campus overview, a ward drill-down and a short-term outlook for the next 24 hours. Elien Jacobs, UX and Frontend Developer, designed the dashboards and ran two rounds of usability sessions with bed managers and head nurses.

The rollout was staged: the first campus went live in September, the remaining two in October after the ward mapping was validated with the bed management office.

## 4. Adoption: the whiteboard problem

The main issue was not technical. Day shifts adopted the dashboard quickly, but the night shift nurses kept using the whiteboard at the nursing station. Their feedback was simple: at 3 a.m. nobody logs in to a laptop to check a report, while the whiteboard is just there on the wall.

Rather than pushing training, Elien designed a large-screen view per ward: a simplified, auto-refreshing page showing beds as coloured tiles, readable from across the corridor, running on a wall-mounted screen. After a two-week trial on one internal medicine ward, Jeroen's team ordered screens for the other wards. Whiteboard usage has largely stopped, although a few wards keep one for notes that do not belong in any system, and that is fine.

- Two knowledge transfer sessions held with Jeroen's team (refresh monitoring, adding a ward, changing the outlook logic).
- Kestrel provides best-effort support until the end of January 2024.

## 6. Lessons learned

1. **Design for the actual moment of use.** The large-screen ward view should have been in the original scope; observing a night shift during discovery would have revealed it.
2. **Bed master data is political.** Agreeing which beds "exist" took longer than building the pipelines. Start that conversation in week one.

## Context

The project generates draft discharge letters from sections of the patient record. The DPIA, closed on 2024-03-11, sets binding conditions: no patient data leaves the EU, pseudonymisation before any model call, pseudonymised logging only, and the pseudonymisation key managed by Mediva IT. We need to fix where the model runs, where the pseudonymisation boundary sits and what is logged, before the prototype phase starts on 2024-04-15.

## Options considered

**Option A: Azure OpenAI deployment in an EU region, pseudonymisation inside Mediva's network.**
Record extracts are pseudonymised by a service running in Mediva's environment. Only pseudonymised text crosses to the Azure OpenAI endpoint. Re-identification happens in the same Mediva-side service before the draft is shown.

**Option B: Azure OpenAI deployment in an EU region, pseudonymisation in the cloud application layer.**
Simpler to operate, but identifiable data would sit in an additional cloud component, and the key would need to be reachable from there. Sarah indicated this would require an update of the DPIA.

**Option C: A locally hosted open-weight model on Mediva hardware.**
No data leaves the hospital. Rejected: Mediva has no GPU capacity, the quality of available models for Dutch clinical text was clearly lower in our first tests, and procurement would not fit the project timeline.

## Decision

**Option A.**

- One Azure OpenAI resource in an EU region, in a subscription owned by Mediva. Kestrel works through named accounts that Jeroen's team grants and revokes.

## Decision

**Option A.**

- One Azure OpenAI resource in an EU region, in a subscription owned by Mediva. Kestrel works through named accounts that Jeroen's team grants and revokes.
- The modified abuse-monitoring arrangement requested with Microsoft so that prompts and completions are not retained for human review; confirmation filed with the DPIA.
- No data is used for model training.
- The pseudonymisation and re-identification service runs inside Mediva's environment. The key is managed by Mediva IT; Kestrel has no access.
- Prompts and outputs are logged only after pseudonymisation, with 90 days retention, for quality review.

## Data flow

1. The physician opens the draft function for a stay in the record.
2. The integration reads the relevant sections (admission note, progress notes, lab summary, medication list, specialist reports) from the read-only extract.
3. The pseudonymisation service replaces direct identifiers with pseudonyms and removes free-text identifiers it recognises.
4. The pseudonymised sections and the specialty template go to Azure OpenAI.
5. The draft comes back, is re-identified inside Mediva's environment and shown next to its source sections.
6. The physician edits and signs in the record. The signed letter is never sent back to the model.

## Consequences

- All prompt engineering and evaluation work is done on pseudonymised data. Kestrel engineers never see identifiable content.
- Latency increases by the pseudonymisation step; target is a draft within 30 seconds.
- Any change to steps 2 to 5 is a change to the data flow and goes to Sarah before implementation (kickoff decision D3).
- Costs: model consumption is billed directly to Mediva. We will report token usage per letter from the prototype phase onwards so Jeroen can estimate yearly cost.

## Open points

- Residual identifier rate after pseudonymisation: Amira reports on 2024-04-05.

## 1. Purpose

Action item 3 of the DPIA closure meeting (2024-03-11): test the pseudonymisation on 200 sample letters and report the residual identifier rate. The test was run inside Mediva's environment. The review of residual identifiers was done by a Mediva IT staff member with access to the identifiable source, together with me looking only at the pseudonymised output and the position markers. No identifiable content left Mediva's environment or appears in this report.

## 2. Method

**Sample.** 200 discharge letters from 2023, 100 from internal medicine and 100 from geriatrics, randomly selected by Mediva IT, together with the record sections the letters were based on (about 1,900 text sections in total).

**Pseudonymisation pipeline (version 0.3).**
1. Rule-based pass for structured identifiers: national register number, patient number, dates of birth, phone numbers, postal addresses, email addresses.
2. Named-entity model for free text: person names, places, institutions.
3. Dictionary pass with the names of Mediva staff, which are kept as role labels ("treating physician") rather than names.
4. Dates are shifted by a per-stay offset, so intervals stay correct ("day 3 of admission") but the real dates do not reach the model.

**Review.** Every remaining token that could identify a patient was marked by the reviewer and categorised as *direct* (name, number, exact address) or *indirect* (a combination that could point to a person: a rare occupation, a family relation with a role, a small village).

## Participants

Four physicians from internal medicine (two staff members, two assistants), three from geriatrics (two staff, one assistant), a medical secretary from geriatrics, Dr. Hilde Van Damme (first half hour), Pieter De Smet and Amira El Idrissi (Kestrel).

## 1. Goal

Agree on the structure of the draft letter per specialty, and on what the draft should and should not contain. We used 20 historical letters per department, viewed through the pseudonymised flow, as examples.

## 2. What a good letter looks like

The group agreed that the general practitioner reads the letter in under two minutes and is looking for four things: why the patient was admitted, what was done, what changed in the medication, and what the GP needs to do next. Everything else is secondary.

Common structure, both departments:

1. Reason for admission (two or three sentences)
2. Relevant history (short, only what matters for this stay)
3. Course of stay (per problem, not per day)
4. Key results (lab, imaging, only abnormal or decisive results)
5. Medication at discharge, with changes marked: started, stopped, dose changed, with reason
6. Follow-up: appointments, instructions for the GP, pending results

## 3. Differences per specialty

**Internal medicine**
- Course of stay per problem is essential; multi-problem stays are common.
- Pending results must be explicit ("culture result pending, will be communicated").

**Geriatrics**
- Functional status at admission and discharge (mobility, cognition, falls) is a mandatory paragraph.

# Design Note: Section Selection and Prompt Structure

| | |
|---|---|
| **Customer** | Mediva Care Group |
| **Project** | Discharge Letter Summarisation |
| **Document type** | Technical design note |
| **Date** | 2024-05-10 |
| **Author** | Pieter De Smet, Lead AI Architect, Kestrel Consulting |
| **Reviewers** | Amira El Idrissi; Jeroen Lambrecht (integration part) |

## 1. Problem

A stay in internal medicine produces on average 60 to 80 record sections; long geriatric stays easily exceed 200. Sending everything to the model in one prompt is slow, expensive, and in our first tests on 50 historical stays it produced vague course-of-stay paragraphs: the model summarised the most recent notes and forgot the first week. This note describes the two-step approach used from sprint P2 onwards.

## 2. Step 1: select and condense sections

**Selection rules (deterministic, in code):**

- Always included: admission note, discharge medication list, admission medication list, last progress note, consult reports of other specialties, the lab summary table.
- Progress notes: one per day maximum, preferring the note of the treating physician over nursing notes.
- Imaging and procedure reports: only the conclusion paragraph.
- Excluded: administrative notes, scanned documents without text (flagged), duplicated copies of the same report.

**Condensation per problem.** For stays with more than 40 selected sections, a first model call condenses the progress notes per problem, using the problem list of the stay as headings. Each condensed sentence keeps a reference to the section it came from. This intermediate result is never shown to the physician as such; it is input for step 2.

## 3. Step 2: draft the letter

The second call receives:

1. The specialty template (internal medicine or geriatrics, from the workshop of 2024-04-26)
2. Instructions on style: Dutch, one page target, no stronger wording than the source, no advice not present in the notes
