# Lunch and Learn: Evaluating a Knowledge Assistant with Clinicians

| | |
|---|---|
| **Organisation** | Kestrel Consulting (internal) |
| **Date** | 2026-10-23, 12:15 to 13:30 (kennisdeling session) |
| **Location** | Kestrel office Ghent, big room, and Teams |
| **Author / presenter** | Amira El Idrissi, Lead AI Engineer |
| **Document type** | Internal session notes |

## Context

This session used the **Clinical Knowledge Assistant** at Mediva Care Group as a case. The assistant, built on Microsoft Foundry with a Foundry IQ knowledge base and Azure OpenAI, answers questions from physicians and nurses based on Mediva's own clinical guidelines and protocols, always with a reference to the source. It is in pilot in the **cardiology** and **emergency** departments.

The talk was not about the architecture. It was about one question: how do you know whether a clinical assistant is good enough?

## 1. Build the evaluation set with the people who will use it

The evaluation set now contains **200 questions**, written and reviewed with clinicians from both pilot departments. Every question has:
- a reference answer, written by a clinician
- the expected source document and section
- a tag for the department and the type of question (dosing, procedure, contraindication, organisation)

Practical tips that worked:
- Sessions of 45 minutes at most, with coffee, in the department rather than in a meeting room.
- Ask clinicians for the questions they actually asked a colleague last week, not for "test questions". The second kind is always too easy.
- Let a second clinician review every reference answer. Disagreements between clinicians are information, not noise.

## 2. Score what matters

We rate every answer on three things: correct and complete, partially correct, or incorrect / wrong source. A correct answer from the wrong source counts as wrong. In a clinical setting, the source is part of the answer, because the clinician must be able to check it.

# FinOps Tips, Part 2: The Cost of AI Workloads

| | |
|---|---|
| **Organisation** | Kestrel Consulting (internal) |
| **Date** | 2026-11-13 |
| **Author** | Jonas Peeters, Cloud Platform Engineer |
| **Document type** | Internal guideline (FinOps tips, part 2), presented at the November kennisdeling |

## Why part 2

Part 1 (September 2024) was about idle compute, tags and budgets. Those rules still apply. But our cost profile has changed: on generative AI and agent work, the bill is driven less by virtual machines and clusters and more by model tokens, search capacity and evaluation runs. These are harder to predict and easier to waste. Below is what we have learned.

## 1. Make token cost visible from sprint 1

- Every model call logs input tokens, output tokens, model name and the feature that made the call (chat answer, query planning, summarisation, evaluation).
- Build a simple cost dashboard per environment in the first sprint: cost per day, per feature and per 100 user questions. The tech radar already says this; this is how.
- Report "cost per answered question" in the status report. Customers understand that number much better than a monthly total.

## 2. Pick the smallest model that passes the evaluation

- Start with a smaller, cheaper model for each step and move up only if the evaluation set shows it is needed.
- Query rewriting, classification and routing rarely need the largest model. The final answer sometimes does.
- Re-check the choice when new model versions come out. A newer small model often beats the older large one.

## 3. Control the context

- Retrieval returns too much by default. Fewer, better passages lower cost and usually improve answers.
- Trim conversation history: keep a summary of earlier turns instead of the full transcript.
- System prompts grow over a project like ivy on a wall. Review them every few sprints; remove instructions that no longer change the evaluation results.

## 4. Agents: watch the loops

# Data Mapping Note: ADT Events to Bed Model

| | |
|---|---|
| **Customer** | Mediva Care Group |
| **Project** | Bed Capacity Dashboard |
| **Document type** | Data mapping note |
| **Date** | 2023-06-09 |
| **Author** | Sofie Claes, Senior Data Engineer, Kestrel Consulting |
| **Version** | 0.9 (for review by Mediva IT) |

## 1. Purpose

This note describes how admission, discharge and transfer (ADT) events from the hospital information system are mapped to the bed-level model in Azure Synapse Analytics. It is the basis for the Power BI reports and for the definitions agreed in the workshop of 2023-05-24. No patient-identifying attributes are loaded; the patient is represented only by a stay key generated in the extract.

## 2. Source

The ADT extract is delivered by Mediva IT as files every 15 minutes, containing all events since the previous file. Each event has: event type, event timestamp, recorded timestamp, stay key, campus code, ward code, room code, bed code, specialty code and, for discharges, the planned discharge date.

Observed volume in the test month: about 9,000 events per day across the three campuses.

## 3. Event mapping

| Source event | Meaning | Effect on bed model |
|---|---|---|
| A01 admit | Patient admitted to a bed | Bed becomes occupied |
| A02 transfer | Patient moves to another bed | Old bed free, new bed occupied |
| A03 discharge | Patient discharged | Bed becomes free |
| A08 update | Data update, often planned discharge date | Update outlook only |
| A11 cancel admit | Admission cancelled | Revert to previous state |
| A12 cancel transfer | Transfer cancelled | Revert both beds |
| A13 cancel discharge | Discharge cancelled | Bed occupied again |

The cancel events are the tricky part: about 2% of events are cancellations, sometimes arriving hours later. The model therefore rebuilds the state of the last 72 hours on every run instead of applying events one by one.

## 4. Blocked beds

Blocked beds are not ADT events.

sometimes arriving hours later. The model therefore rebuilds the state of the last 72 hours on every run instead of applying events one by one.

## 4. Blocked beds

Blocked beds are not ADT events. They are recorded in a separate bed status table in the hospital information system, with a free-text reason field. In the sample of 1,400 blocks:

- 61% had a recognisable reason ("isolatie", "onderhoud", "defect", "gereserveerd")
- 27% had an empty reason
- 12% had something else ("zie dokter", "familie", initials of a nurse)

Mapping to the four agreed reasons is done with a keyword list maintained by the bed management office. Empty and unrecognised reasons map to "other". I propose that the bed management office reviews the "other" list monthly; without that, the category will grow.

## 5. Master data: the bed list

The official bed list from facility management contains 1,118 beds. In the ADT events of the test month we saw 1,163 distinct bed codes. The difference:

- 29 bed codes that are corridor or overflow beds used during peaks
- 11 codes for beds that were removed during a renovation but are still used in the system
- 5 codes that look like typing errors

Proposal: the model uses the official list as reference and shows unknown bed codes in a separate "unmapped" table that the bed management office reviews. Overflow beds get a flag and appear in the overview only when occupied. This needs confirmation from the bed management office before the first go-live.

## 6. Timing and late events

Event timestamp and recorded timestamp can differ by several hours, especially for night-time discharges entered the next morning. The dashboard uses the recorded timestamp for the current state (what the system knows now) and shows a "last update" time per ward, so users understand why a ward lags behind.

## 7. Open questions for Mediva IT

1. Can the extract include the bed status table changes in the same 15-minute delivery? (Today it is delivered daily.)

# Design Note: Refresh Architecture and Performance

| | |
|---|---|
| **Customer** | Mediva Care Group |
| **Project** | Bed Capacity Dashboard |
| **Document type** | Technical design note |
| **Date** | 2023-07-14 |
| **Author** | Sofie Claes, Senior Data Engineer, Kestrel Consulting |
| **Reviewers** | Jeroen Lambrecht (Mediva IT), Elien Jacobs |

## 1. Context

The first Power BI report on the Synapse model was shown to bed managers on 2023-07-07. The content was well received, but two technical concerns came up: the report sometimes showed figures that were 30 minutes old instead of 15, and the ward drill-down took up to 12 seconds to open. This note describes the changes to the refresh chain and the model to fix both.

## 2. Refresh chain before the change

1. ADT file lands every 15 minutes.
2. Synapse pipeline is triggered on a fixed schedule (:00, :15, :30, :45) and rebuilds the bed state for the last 72 hours.
3. Power BI dataset refresh scheduled on its own fixed schedule.

Because the file delivery, the pipeline and the dataset refresh each ran on independent schedules, a file arriving at :16 was only processed at :30 and visible after the dataset refresh at :45 or later.

## 3. Changes

**3.1 Event-driven pipeline.** The Synapse pipeline now starts when a new ADT file arrives, instead of on a fixed schedule. A guard prevents two runs in parallel; if a file arrives during a run, the next run picks it up.

**3.2 Dataset refresh triggered by the pipeline.** At the end of a successful run, the pipeline triggers the Power BI dataset refresh. If the pipeline fails, the dataset keeps the last good state and the report shows the "last update" time in orange after 30 minutes.

**3.3 Smaller dataset.** The report does not need the full event history. The Power BI dataset now contains only:

- the current state per bed (about 1,160 rows)
- the 24-hour outlook per ward
- daily occupancy snapshots for the last 90 days

# ADR-01: Knowledge Base Design with Foundry IQ

| | |
|---|---|
| **Customer** | Mediva Care Group |
| **Project** | Clinical Knowledge Assistant |
| **Document type** | Architecture decision record |
| **Date** | 2026-02-06 |
| **Author** | Pieter De Smet, Lead AI Architect, Kestrel Consulting |
| **Status** | Accepted |
| **Reviewed by** | Amira El Idrissi; Jeroen Lambrecht (Mediva IT) |

## Context

The assistant must answer clinical staff questions only from Mediva-approved guidelines and protocols, cite document, version and date, and say so when the sources do not answer the question. Questions are often compound: "What is the protocol for chest pain with suspected dissection in a patient on anticoagulants, and when do we call cardiology?" touches two departments and three documents. The SOW names a Foundry IQ knowledge base with agentic retrieval; this ADR records how we set it up and why.

## Options considered

**Option A: Hand-built retrieval pipeline.** Our own chunking, embedding, ranking and a single retrieval call per question, orchestrated in code. Full control, but we would rebuild query planning and multi-source merging ourselves, and own all of it after handover.

**Option B: Foundry IQ knowledge base with agentic retrieval.** Knowledge sources per source library, a knowledge base on top, and agentic retrieval that plans sub-queries, runs them over the sources and returns grounded results with references. The assistant in Microsoft Foundry uses the knowledge base as its retrieval layer and an Azure OpenAI model to write the answer.

**Option C: Long-context prompting.** Put the relevant department's guidelines in the prompt. Rejected: emergency alone has about 340 documents, cost per question would be high, and citations would be unreliable.

## Decision

**Option B.**

- One knowledge base for the pilot, with separate knowledge sources for the intranet library export, the confirmed legacy documents and the emergency nursing procedures.

## Decision

**Option B.**

- One knowledge base for the pilot, with separate knowledge sources for the intranet library export, the confirmed legacy documents and the emergency nursing procedures.
- Agentic retrieval enabled; the retrieval instructions tell the planner to prefer documents of the department the user selects in the front end, without excluding others.
- Answer generation with an Azure OpenAI chat model deployed in the EU region, from the Microsoft Foundry project.
- Every result carries document title, version, publication date and link; the answer instructions require at least one citation per statement and an explicit "not found in Mediva sources" when retrieval returns nothing relevant.
- All resources in Mediva's subscription in an EU region.

## Metadata as filters

The knowledge sources carry department, document type, version and review date as filterable fields. Where the metadata is missing, Amira's ingestion step derives version and date from the cover page or file name and marks the field as "derived". Of the 550 cardiology and emergency documents analysed, version information was missing or ambiguous for about 18%.

This matters because the assistant can only show the right version if the index knows it. Derived values are a stopgap, not a substitute for owners confirming the current version.

## Consequences

- Less custom code to hand over; query planning behaviour depends on the platform and must be covered by the evaluation set.
- Retrieval behaviour can change with platform updates. We pin settings where possible and rerun the full evaluation set after every change to sources, instructions or model deployment.
- Consumption has two parts: retrieval (query planning plus searches) and answer generation. We will report both per question from the first demo, so Jeroen can forecast.
- Agentic retrieval adds latency compared with a single search. Target: answer start within 6 seconds, complete within 15 seconds for 90% of questions.

MAPE is computed on containers with a dwell time of at least 6 hours, as agreed during data discovery. The P10–P90 range contains the actual gate-out in 79% of cases, close to the intended 80%.

The reefer issue from the last sprint review was real: reefer containers in the inspection zone were not getting the inspection flag because their yard moves use a different block prefix. Fixed on 2024-01-10 as a documented bug fix; the hold-out continues with that fix.

## 3. Case review

Each planner brought five containers where they thought the forecast was "wrong". We reviewed 20 cases together:

# ADR-03: Daily Batch Scoring, Intraday Refresh Deferred

| | |
|---|---|
| **Customer** | Scaldis Logistics |
| **Project** | Container Dwell-Time Forecasting |
| **Date** | 2024-02-09 |
| **Author** | Amira El Idrissi, ML Engineer, Kestrel Consulting |
| **Document type** | Architecture decision record |
| **Status** | Accepted (Nathalie Dumont, product owner, 2024-02-09) |
| **Related** | ADR-01 storage zones, ADR-02 point-in-time feature snapshots |

## Context

The proposal describes a daily batch forecast to begin with and an intraday refresh as an option. Planners now use the 05:30 forecast for the morning plan. During the evaluation workshop on 2024-01-19, two planners asked whether the forecast could refresh at noon, when many customs releases come in.

Current pipeline:
- TOS export lands in Azure Data Lake Storage Gen2 at 01:00;
- curated and feature jobs in Databricks finish around 03:20;
- batch scoring in Azure Machine Learning starts at 05:00 and writes the output table by 05:30.

The TOS export is a nightly file. There is no near-real-time event feed today. The TOS update announced by the vendor does not add one.

## Options considered

1. **Keep daily batch only.** Simple, already in production, fully covered by the runbook.
2. **Second batch at noon from a partial export.** Requires a second export from the TOS reporting module at 11:30. The TOS administrator says this export puts load on the TOS database during the busiest hours, and the vendor advises against it.
3. **Intraday scoring from an event stream.** Requires an event feed from the TOS, which does not exist. Would mean a different ingestion design and new integration work with the TOS vendor.

## Decision

Option 1. The forecast is scored once a day, available at 05:30. Intraday refresh is deferred until the TOS can provide events in near real time. Recorded as a recommendation in the closing report.

# Workshop Notes: Gate and Yard Events

| | |
|---|---|
| **Customer** | Scaldis Logistics |
| **Project** | Container Dwell-Time Forecasting |
| **Date** | 2023-09-21 |
| **Location** | Scaldis terminal, planning office, first floor |
| **Author** | Sofie Claes, Senior Data Engineer, Kestrel Consulting |
| **Document type** | Workshop notes |

## Participants

Nathalie Dumont (product owner), two yard planners from the day shift, the Scaldis TOS administrator, Sofie Claes, Bram Visser (DataForge), Amira El Idrissi.

## Purpose

Understand which events in the terminal operating system (TOS) mark the start and the end of a container's stay, and how reliable each event is in practice. The result feeds data contract v0.1.

## 1. Lifecycle of an import container

The planners walked us through a typical import box, on a whiteboard:

1. **Vessel discharge**: quay crane moves the container to the yard. Event recorded automatically by the crane system and pushed to the TOS.
2. **Yard moves**: zero or more reshuffles. Recorded by straddle carrier drivers on their terminals.
3. **Customs release**: status update from the customs channel. Arrival time varies a lot.
4. **Truck appointment**: the haulier books a slot. Not always used.
5. **Gate-out**: the truck leaves with the box. This ends the dwell period.

For export and empty containers the sequence starts with a **gate-in** at the truck gate. Gate-in also matters for imports that go back in after inspection. The planners agreed that dwell time is measured from discharge (or gate-in) to gate-out, in hours.

## 2. Known quirks (planner view)

- "At the truck gate, sometimes the OCR camera and the clerk both register the box." The planners believe this causes double gate-in records, mostly at lanes 4 and 5.
- During gate outages, clerks register containers afterwards in a batch, or not at all, and the first trace is a yard move.

# Design Note: Feature Pipelines and Storage Layout

| | |
|---|---|
| **Customer** | Scaldis Logistics |
| **Project** | Container Dwell-Time Forecasting |
| **Date** | 2023-10-20 |
| **Author** | Bram Visser, Databricks Specialist, DataForge (subcontractor to Kestrel Consulting) |
| **Document type** | Technical design note |
| **Reviewers** | Sofie Claes, Amira El Idrissi |

## 1. Purpose

Describe how TOS events flow from the nightly export to the feature tables used for training and scoring, so that the operations analytics team at Scaldis can maintain the pipelines after handover.

## 2. Storage layout in Azure Data Lake Storage Gen2

One storage account, hierarchical namespace enabled, three containers:

| Container | Content | Retention | Who writes |
|---|---|---|---|
| `raw` | Nightly TOS export files as delivered, partitioned by export date | 5 years | Transfer job only |
| `curated` | Cleaned events: UTC timestamps, carrier aliases mapped, visit IDs resolved | 5 years | Databricks curated jobs |
| `features` | One row per container visit per snapshot date | 2 years | Databricks feature jobs |

Raw files are never modified. Every correction lives in curated and is traceable to a rule with an ID, so planners and the TOS administrator can see why a record changed.

Access: the Databricks workspace reads and writes through a managed identity; individual users get read-only access to curated and features. Scaldis IT asked not to use account keys, which we follow.

## 3. Jobs and schedule

| Job | Start | Typical duration | Depends on |
|---|---|---|---|
| Transfer TOS export to raw | 01:00 | 10 min | TOS export server |
| Curated events | 02:00 | 25 min | raw |
| Feature snapshot | 02:45 | 35 min | curated |
| Scoring (Azure ML, later) | 05:00 | 15 min | features |

The goal is a forecast available to planners before the 06:00 shift change. Jobs run on job clusters that terminate when done; no all-purpose cluster is left running at night.

## 1. Who we design for

Based on two mornings of shadowing on the terminal (28 and 30 January), three user groups:

| Group | Context | What they need |
|---|---|---|
| Shift leaders | Office and on the quay, phone in hand, interrupted every few minutes | Short, certain answers; who to call |
| Planners | Desktop, several screens, Teams always open | Exact steps, links to the full SOP |
| New operators and clerks | First months on the job, often on a shared PC in the gate building | Plain explanations, no jargon, reassurance |

Most questions observed were procedural ("what do I do when a reefer alarm goes off during a vessel operation?") and lookup ("which form for a damaged seal?"). Almost nobody asked open questions.

## 2. Principles

1. **Answer first, source always.** The first two lines answer the question. The source link is never optional.
2. **Same language as the question.** Dutch, French or English, detected per message. The source may be in another language; the card then says so.
3. **Short on mobile.** Maximum about 80 words in the card body; "show steps" expands the full procedure.
4. **Never pretend.** If the retrieved passages do not answer the question, the bot says it did not find it and offers the shift leader fallback. No general knowledge answers about terminal operations.
5. **Feedback in one tap.** Thumbs up/down, with an optional reason list on thumbs down.

## 1. Scope of the proof of concept

Action 7 of the kick-off: index one SharePoint site end to end and answer questions over it. We used the "Operations – Quay" site: 214 documents (SOPs, work instructions, checklists), mostly text documents and PDFs, 61% Dutch, 27% French, 12% English.

## 2. Pipeline

1. **Crawl.** An indexing job lists documents in the in-scope libraries through the SharePoint API, using an app identity with read access granted by the site owner. Only published major versions are taken; drafts are skipped.
2. **Extract.** Text and headings are extracted per document. Scanned PDFs without a text layer (9 of 214) are reported to the site owner instead of being processed.
3. **Chunk.** One chunk per section, split on headings; sections longer than about 600 tokens are split on paragraph boundaries with a small overlap. Each chunk keeps the document title, section path, SOP number, language and version date (ADR-01).
4. **Embed and index.** Chunks are embedded with an Azure OpenAI embedding model and written to an Azure AI Search index with both a text field and a vector field.
5. **Refresh.** Nightly incremental run based on the document modified date; deletions detected by comparing the document list.

## 3. Query flow

1. The question from the Teams bot is sent with its detected language.
2. Hybrid query on Azure AI Search: keyword and vector, merged and re-ranked by the semantic ranker; top 5 chunks.
3. Prompt to the Azure OpenAI chat model with the chunks, the instruction to answer only from the chunks and to cite SOP number and section.

# Change Request CR-01: Restricted Operations Libraries in Scope

| | |
|---|---|
| **Customer** | Scaldis Logistics |
| **Project** | Scaldis Ops Copilot |
| **Date** | 2025-03-12 |
| **Author** | Thomas Maes, Project Manager, Kestrel Consulting |
| **Document type** | Change request |
| **Requested by** | Nathalie Dumont, product owner |
| **Decision forum** | Steering committee of 2025-03-20 |

## 1. Request

Add three restricted SharePoint libraries of the operations department to the scope of release 1:

| Library | Approx. documents | Current access |
|---|---|---|
| Incident handling (spills, injuries, quay incidents, evacuation) | 140 | Shift leaders, HSE, management |
| Customs procedures (inspection zone, seals, holds) | 95 | Customs desk, shift leaders, planners |
| Access control (gate exceptions, visitor and contractor access) | 65 | Gate supervisors, security, shift leaders |

Together about 300 documents, on top of the roughly 1,800 documents of the general operations library.

## 2. Reason

During the user tests of the answer cards (week of 24 February), shift leaders asked for incident and gate exception procedures more often than for anything else. Without them, Nathalie expects the copilot to miss the moments where speed matters most, typically at night when no colleague is around to ask.

## 3. Impact analysis

**Functional.** Same answer cards and dialogue flow. The bot must only use restricted documents for users who are allowed to open them in SharePoint.

**Technical.** The three libraries use the same structure as the general library. Indexing is a configuration change. Restricting answers per user requires that the index knows who may read each document and that queries are filtered accordingly. In this CR we propose a first, simpler approach: restricted libraries go into a **separate index**, and the bot queries that index only for users in the SharePoint groups of the library owners. Fine-grained, document-level rules are not foreseen.

## 1. Purpose

A fixed, versioned set of questions that we run after every change to the knowledge base, the retrieval instructions, the answer instructions or the model deployment. The set tells us whether a change makes the assistant better or worse before clinicians notice. It replaces "it looked fine in the demo" with a number we can track.

## 2. Version 1 at a glance

| | Cardiology | Emergency | Cross-department | Total |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Questions | 48 | 52 | 20 | **120** |
| Written by physicians | 30 | 28 | 12 | 70 |
| Written by nurses | 10 | 20 | 6 | 36 |
| Written by coordinators | 8 | 4 | 2 | 14 |

The plan is to grow the set to about 200 questions during the pilot, adding real questions from users (after review and removal of anything patient-related).

## 3. What a question looks like

Each item contains:

- the question, in the words of the person who wrote it, Dutch or English as they asked it
- a reference answer written by the coordinator, short, in action-list form
- the expected source document(s) and the section
- the category (see below)
- critical elements: facts that must be in the answer (for example a dose, a threshold, a time limit)

Example (emergency): "What do I prepare for a patient with suspected sepsis in the waiting room?" Reference: the steps of the emergency sepsis protocol, expected source: the current sepsis protocol, critical elements: the time target for antibiotics and the lactate measurement.

# Acceptance Criteria Note: Accuracy Thresholds per Field

| | |
|---|---|
| **Customer** | Scaldis Logistics |
| **Project** | Customs Document Extraction |
| **Date** | 2025-10-30 |
| **Author** | Amira El Idrissi, ML Engineer, Kestrel Consulting |
| **Document type** | Acceptance criteria note |
| **Approved by** | Jan Wouters, product owner (sprint 2 review, 2025-10-31) |

## 1. Purpose

The statement of work says phase 1 is accepted when the agreed document types meet accuracy thresholds set with Jan Wouters in sprint 2. This note defines how accuracy is measured and which thresholds apply.

## 2. Definitions

- **Field-level accuracy:** share of fields on the test set where the extracted value equals the value confirmed by a customs agent, after normalisation (spaces, date format, decimal separator). An empty extraction where a value exists counts as an error.
- **Test set:** per document type, at least 20 labelled documents that were never used for training, drawn from different senders. Refreshed every quarter with recent documents.
- **Weighted accuracy (all types):** field-level accuracy weighted by the weekly volume of each type, so the figure reflects the actual workload at the desk.
- **Confidence:** the confidence score returned by Azure AI Document Intelligence per field. Used for routing, not for measuring accuracy.

## 3. Thresholds

| Field category | Threshold (field-level accuracy) | Below threshold |
|---|---|---|
| Critical fields (container number, HS code, gross weight, number of packages, UN number and class, seal number) | 97% | Field always highlighted for review |
| Standard fields (names, addresses, dates, references) | 92% | Field shown, review advised |
| Line items (descriptions, quantities, values) | 90% per column | Review per line |

## 1. Purpose

Phase 1 does not submit anything to the customs declaration system. Agents still create the declaration themselves, from a validated export instead of from paper. This note maps every extracted field to the data element the agent needs and defines the export layout.

## 2. Principles

- One export record per container, combining all validated documents for that container.
- Field names in the export follow the names the customs agents use in the declaration screens, not the names on the source documents.
- Values are normalised (dates ISO, weights in kg with a dot as decimal separator, country codes ISO 3166 alpha-2).
- Each exported value keeps a reference to its source document and page, so an agent can always go back to the original.
- When two documents disagree (for example gross weight on the invoice and on the packing list), both values are exported and the conflict is flagged. The agent decides.

## 1. Why this test

Risk R-14: document-level permission trimming (ADR-03) adds a group lookup and a security filter to every query. Pilot users are used to a median answer time of about 3 seconds. Nathalie Dumont set the acceptable limit for go-live at a median below 5 seconds and a 95th percentile below 10 seconds, measured from the moment the user sends the question in Microsoft Teams until the answer card appears.

## 2. Set-up

- Test environment with a full copy of the production index: about 2,100 documents (general and restricted libraries), with permissions synced from SharePoint.
- 12 test accounts with different roles, from a gate clerk (few groups) to an operations manager (64 group memberships).
- Load script replaying 500 questions from the pilot logs (pseudonymised), at 1, 5 and 15 questions per second. 15 per second is about five times the expected peak at shift change.
- Timings logged per step: bot receive, group lookup, search, model call, card rendering.

## 3. First run (2 July)

| Load | Median | P95 | Errors |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 q/s | 5.6 s | 10.9 s | 0 |
| 5 q/s | 5.9 s | 11.8 s | 0 |
| 15 q/s | 7.4 s | 16.2 s | 2.1% (rate limit on model calls) |

Breakdown at 5 q/s (median): group lookup 1.4 s, search 0.6 s, model call 3.3 s, rest 0.6 s. The group lookup was the new cost: for every question we resolved the user's groups from scratch, because the 15-minute cache from ADR-03 was not yet active in the test build.

## 4. Changes

1. **Group cache switched on** (15 minutes, as designed). Lookup drops to near zero for repeated questions; the first question of a session still pays the cost.

## 1. Why in sprint 1

The statement of work puts the architecture and security review in sprint 1, before any document is processed. After the Ops Copilot, nobody at Scaldis or Kestrel wanted to repeat a late review.

## 2. Target architecture (as presented)

1. **Intake.** Two channels: the customs desk shared mailbox (attachments from forwarders, hauliers and shipping lines) and the scanning station at the customs desk (paper documents brought by drivers).
2. **Orchestration.** An Azure Logic Apps workflow picks up each new document, stores the original, calls classification and extraction, and puts the result in the validation queue.
3. **Classification and extraction.** Azure AI Document Intelligence: a custom classifier to recognise the document type, then a custom extraction model per type, combined in a composed model.
4. **Validation screen.** Customs agents see the document and the extracted fields side by side, confirm or correct, and release the record.
5. **Output.** Validated fields are exported as a structured file per container for the customs agents to use in the declaration system. No automatic submission in phase 1.

# ADR-03: Document-Level Permission Trimming at Query Time

| | |
|---|---|
| **Customer** | Scaldis Logistics |
| **Project** | Scaldis Ops Copilot |
| **Date** | 2025-06-06 |
| **Author** | Pieter De Smet, Lead AI Architect, Kestrel Consulting |
| **Document type** | Architecture decision record |
| **Status** | Accepted (reviewed by Wim Goossens, 2025-06-05) |
| **Supersedes** | Restricted-index approach described in CR-01 |
| **Related** | ADR-01 chunking strategy, ADR-02 answer language and citations, security finding H-01 |

## Context

Security finding H-01 requires that a user only receives answers based on documents they are allowed to open in SharePoint. About one in five documents in the restricted libraries, and a small number in the general library, have unique permissions. The separate restricted index proposed in CR-01 filters per library and is therefore insufficient.

## Options

1. **Query-time check per result.** Retrieve as today, then check for every candidate document whether the user can open it, by calling SharePoint at query time. Accurate, but adds several calls per question and makes latency depend on SharePoint response times.
2. **Security filter in the index.** Store the allowed principals (users and groups) per document on every chunk in Azure AI Search, and filter every query on the user's identity and group memberships. Requires a sync of permissions.
3. **One index per permission set.** Not realistic with hundreds of distinct permission sets.

## Decision

Option 2, with a fail-closed rule.

- **Indexing.** For each document the indexing job reads the effective read permissions from SharePoint and resolves SharePoint groups to the directory groups and users they contain. The list of allowed principal IDs is written to a filterable field on every chunk of that document.
- **Sync.** An hourly job processes permission changes since the last run; a nightly reconciliation compares the full permission set for all documents.

## 4. Main issue: handwritten annotations on CMR notes

**Handwritten annotations on CMR consignment notes are the main accuracy issue.** Truck drivers and warehouse staff often write corrections, seal numbers or remarks on the CMR by hand, sometimes over the printed fields. | | |
|---|---|
| **Customer** | Scaldis Logistics |
| **Project** | Customs Document Extraction |
| **Date** | 2026-07-10 |
| **Author** | Amira El Idrissi, Lead AI Engineer, Kestrel Consulting |

| **Period** | Sprints 19 and 20 (2026-06-15 to 2026-07-10) |
| **Reviewed with** | Jan Wouters, Pieter De Smet (2026-07-09) |

## 1. Background

Handwritten annotations on CMR consignment notes are the main accuracy issue of the project. At the June status report, field-level accuracy on CMR was 86%, against more than 95% for most printed types. On 2026-06-04 Jan Wouters agreed to two measures:

- **Option 2, immediately:** CMR notes with detected handwriting in an extracted field are marked "always review" for that field. Implemented on 2026-06-18.
- **Option 1, as an experiment:** a separate handwriting-aware model for the three most affected fields: seal number, remarks and date of delivery.

This report covers the experiment.

## 2. Set-up

- 620 CMR notes with handwriting, labelled with the "handwritten" flag since January, of which 470 for training and 150 for testing. The test set includes documents from 40 different hauliers.
- A second custom extraction model in Azure AI Document Intelligence, trained only on CMR notes with handwriting and only on the three target fields, using the service's handwriting recognition.
- In the Azure Logic Apps workflow, CMR notes flagged with handwriting are sent to both the standard CMR model and the handwriting model. For the three fields, the value with the higher confidence wins; all other fields come from the standard model.

## 3. Results on the test set (150 CMR notes with handwriting)

| Field | Standard model | Handwriting model | Combined rule |
|---|---|---|---|
| Seal number | 71% | 87% | 89% |
| Date of delivery | 78% | 90% | 91% |
| Remarks (free text, character level ≥ 90% similar) | 52% | 57% | 58% |

## 1. What the pipeline does

Documents arrive in the customs shared mailbox or the scanning station folder. An Azure Logic Apps workflow stores the original, calls the classifier and the composed extraction model in Azure AI Document Intelligence, checks values against reference lists and places the result in the validation queue. Customs agents validate every document. Nothing is sent to the declaration system automatically.

## 2. Daily checks (first line, 07:30)

| Check | Where | Normal | Action if not normal |
|---|---|---|---|
| Failed workflow runs overnight | Logic Apps run history, filter "Failed" | 0–3 | See 3.1 |
| Validation queue age | Queue dashboard on the validation screen | Oldest item < 30 min in office hours | Inform desk coordinator |
| Manual folder | Scanning share, folder "manual" | < 20 new items | Inform desk coordinator |
| Retention job | Last run status | Succeeded, ran at 02:00 | See 3.5 |

Alerts already mail the desk coordinator and Kestrel for failures longer than 30 minutes and for queue age above 30 minutes.

## 3. Procedures

### 3.1 Failed workflow run
1. Open the failed run and read the failing action.
2. **Extraction call returned "too many requests"**: the workflow retries four times with increasing delay. If it still fails, resubmit the run. If many runs fail, check whether a large batch arrived (for example 300 scans at once) and resubmit in groups of 50.
3. **Mailbox connection failed**: usually an expired or changed permission on the shared mailbox. Contact the Scaldis messaging team;

# ADR-02: Resample Sensor Signals to 10-Second Intervals in the Silver Layer

| | |
|---|---|
| **Customer** | Verhaeghe Foods |
| **Project** | Line Sensor Data Platform |
| **Date** | 2024-08-02 |
| **Author** | Bram Visser, Databricks Specialist, DataForge (subcontracted by Kestrel Consulting) |
| **Document type** | Architecture decision record |
| **Status** | Accepted (reviewed by Sofie Claes and Dries Callens on 2024-08-01) |

## Context

The line PLCs produce signals at very different rates. Blancher temperatures and belt speeds arrive every second, freezer zone temperatures every one to five seconds, energy meters every 15 seconds, and packaging counters only when something happens. Line 1 alone gives about 235 tags. At source frequency, six lines produce several hundred million rows per month.

The quality team does not need one-second detail for its main questions (batch traceability, range checks, shift comparison). It does need to see short excursions, for example a blancher that drops two degrees for half a minute after a restart.

ADR-01 already fixed the layering: raw telemetry lands unchanged in the bronze layer of the Microsoft Fabric lakehouse, and transformations run in Databricks notebooks on the same storage.

## Options considered

1. **Keep source frequency in silver.** Simple, no information lost. Large tables, slow queries for every report, and every consumer must handle irregular timestamps.
2. **Resample to 1 minute.** Small and fast, but a 30-second excursion disappears into an average.
3. **Resample to 10 seconds, with min, max and mean per interval.** About ten times fewer rows than source, keeps short excursions visible through min and max.
4. **Different interval per signal type.** Most precise, but harder to explain and to join.

## Decision

Option 3. The silver layer holds one row per tag per 10-second interval, with:

- `value_mean`, `value_min`, `value_max`, `sample_count`

We walked line 3 from the freezer exit to packaging between 07:45 and 09:30.

**Freezer exit.** Product leaves the tunnel freezer at around −18 °C. There is visible fog for about two metres after the exit, and frost forms on every cold surface. Dries' concern from the kickoff is justified: a camera here would see fog for most of the shift. Rejected.

**Vibrating transfer belt, about six metres after the exit.** The fog is gone, product is spread in a thin layer, belt speed is constant per product. ## 3. Chosen position: technical notes

- Camera on a stainless gantry above the transfer belt, about 80 cm above the product, looking straight down.

# Workshop Notes: Defect Class Definitions

| | |
|---|---|
| **Customer** | Verhaeghe Foods |
| **Project** | Quality Inspection Vision |
| **Date** | 2025-03-28 |
| **Author** | Amira El Idrissi, ML Engineer and project lead, Kestrel Consulting |
| **Document type** | Workshop notes |
| **Participants** | Dries Callens, the two quality team members assigned to labelling, Amira El Idrissi, Ruben Wouters |

## 1. Purpose

Agree on clear definitions for the four defect classes of version 1, with example photos, so that labels are consistent. Kickoff action item 4.

Dries brought 60 photos from complaint files and spot checks. Ruben joined to understand how the labelling tool must present classes.

## 2. Definitions agreed

### Foreign material (FM)

Anything that is not the product: stones, wood, plastic, metal, insects, leaves of another crop. Also stems longer than 2 cm for peas and beans.

- Label even when very small, as long as it is visible.
- Pieces of product's own leaf (for spinach) are *not* FM.

### Discolouration (DC)

A piece whose colour is clearly outside normal for the product: brown or black spots larger than about 3 mm, yellowing on green products, grey surfaces from freezer burn.

- Natural colour variation between pieces is *not* a defect.
- This was the hardest class to agree on. The two labellers disagreed on 9 out of 20 example photos. We agreed to mark doubtful cases as "uncertain" rather than force a choice.

### Clumps (CL)

Two or more pieces frozen together into a lump larger than about three times a normal piece. Clumps lead to wrong pack weights and customer complaints.

- Small clumps of two pieces are not labelled in version 1.

### Packaging damage (PD)

Torn or open film, bags with a bad seal visible at the packaging machine infeed side. Version 1 will only see what is visible from the camera position chosen on the line walk.

## 3. Labelling rules

1. Draw a box around each defect. One box per object.

# Design Note: Labelling Tool, Version 1

| | |
|---|---|
| **Customer** | Verhaeghe Foods |
| **Project** | Quality Inspection Vision |
| **Date** | 2025-04-11 |
| **Author** | Ruben Wouters, Junior Developer, Kestrel Consulting |
| **Document type** | Technical design note |
| **Reviewed by** | Amira El Idrissi |

## 1. Goal

Let Dries Callens' quality team label images from the inspection points themselves, quickly and consistently, without installing software. The plan is 4,000 labelled images. With two labellers at about four hours per week each, the tool must make one image take well under a minute on average.

## 2. Users

| Role | What they do |
|---|---|
| Labeller (two people from the quality team) | draw boxes, pick a class, mark OK or uncertain |
| Reviewer (Dries) | review uncertain images, correct labels, see statistics |
| ML engineer (Amira) | export labelled sets for training in Azure AI Vision |

## 3. Main screens

**Queue.** Shows the next image from a randomised queue. Images come from three sources: random captures, images flagged by the model (later, once a model runs), and seeded runs.

**Label view.** The image at full size, the four class buttons with the example photo from the definition sheet, and three actions: *Save*, *OK (no defect)*, *Uncertain*. Keyboard shortcuts: 1 to 4 for classes, O for OK, U for uncertain, Enter to save.

**Review.** For Dries: all uncertain images, with filter per labeller and per class. Dries can accept, change or delete labels.

**Statistics.** Number of labelled images per class against the targets from the workshop of 2025-03-28.

## 4. Data flow

1. The capture module on the edge device saves images on the industrial PC.
2. A selection of images is uploaded to the image store in Verhaeghe's Azure subscription: all flagged images, all seeded runs, and a random sample of 1 in 200 normal images.
3. The labelling tool reads from the image store and writes labels to a small database next to it.

# ADR-02: Image Retention and Personal Data on the Inspection Images

| | |
|---|---|
| **Customer** | Verhaeghe Foods |
| **Project** | Quality Inspection Vision |
| **Date** | 2025-05-05 |
| **Author** | Amira El Idrissi, ML Engineer and project lead, Kestrel Consulting |
| **Document type** | Architecture decision record |
| **Status** | Accepted (Dries Callens and Tine Desmet, 2025-05-05) |

## Context

The camera on line 3 has been capturing images since 2025-04-15. While reviewing the first captures, the quality team noticed that some images show operators' hands and sleeves, and in a few cases a face, when someone leans over the transfer belt to take a sample or clear a blockage.

The images are needed for labelling and retraining. At the same time, images that show identifiable people are personal data, and Verhaeghe's works council was told during the sensor platform project that the plant floor systems do not monitor individual workers. Dries asked for a clear rule before more images are stored.

ADR-01 (inference on the edge with Azure IoT Edge, only flagged images and counts to the cloud) remains valid. This ADR adds retention and privacy rules.

## Options

1. **Store everything, restrict access.** Simple, but keeps images of people for as long as the training set exists.
2. **Blur people automatically before upload.** Requires a second detection step on the edge and still keeps the original on the device.
3. **Crop to the belt area and drop images with a person in view.** The model only needs the belt. Images where something other than product covers part of the belt are not useful for training anyway.

## Decision

Option 3, combined with short retention on the edge.

- The capture module crops every image to the belt area. The belt edges and the gantry frame are outside the crop.
- Images where more than 10% of the belt area is covered by a large non-product object (a hand, an arm, a tool) are discarded on the edge and never uploaded.

# Model Evaluation Report: First Custom Model (v1)

| | |
|---|---|
| **Customer** | Verhaeghe Foods |
| **Project** | Quality Inspection Vision |
| **Date** | 2025-06-16 |
| **Author** | Amira El Idrissi, ML Engineer and project lead, Kestrel Consulting |
| **Document type** | Test and evaluation report |
| **Audience** | Dries Callens, Jonas Peeters, Ruben Wouters |

## 1. Summary

The first custom model was trained in Azure AI Vision on 2025-06-03 on images from line 3. On a held-out test set it reaches **84% defect recall** over all classes, against a project target of 90%. Foreign material is already close to target; packaging damage and clumps are not. The main limits are the number of examples and label consistency on discolouration. We propose a second model before the pilot, not changes to the setup.

## 2. Data

| Set | Images | Of which with defects |
|---|---|---|
| Training | 1,820 | 860 |
| Validation | 230 | 110 |
| Test (held out, never seen in training) | 400 | 190 |

All images come from the line 3 inspection point between 2025-04-15 and 2025-05-30, cropped to the belt as decided in ADR-02. The test set was labelled twice: by one labeller and by Dries.

## 3. How we measure

- **Recall per class:** share of real defects (in Dries' test labels) that the model flags.
- **False positive rate:** share of flags that are not real defects.
- A flag counts as correct if the model box overlaps the labelled box for at least 30%. The operator only needs to know where to look, not the exact outline.
- Threshold: confidence 0.5 for all classes. We will tune per class later.

## 4. Results

| Class | Recall | False positive rate |
|---|---|---|
| Foreign material | 91% | 6% |
| Discolouration | 83% | 14% |
| Clumps | 79% | 9% |
| Packaging damage | 70% | 11% |
| **All classes** | **84%** | **10%** |

Inference time on the industrial PC is 70 to 90 ms per image, well within the capture rate. Jonas' benchmark shows enough spare GPU capacity for a larger model.

## 3. Main issue: lighting on line 3

During the pilot on line 3 in the summer, the model produced many false positives. Analysis showed the cause was **inconsistent lighting**: daylight from the skylights above the line changed during the day, and reflections from the stainless steel frame made healthy product look discoloured. In some hours more than 20% of flags were false.

Solution: Jonas designed a **camera enclosure** for the inspection point, a closed hood with its own LED lighting and a matte inner finish. After the enclosure was installed on line 3, the false positive rate fell to 3.1%. The same enclosure was used on lines 5 and 6 from day one.
